title: A Trump Rally Stuck in Time
excerpt: Photographs by Christopher Lee T he concerns about $4.14-a-gallon gas at the Lincoln Costco an hour and a half to the east? The worries about the war in Iran, t
body: Photographs by Christopher Lee T he concerns about $4.14-a-gallon gas at the Lincoln Costco an hour and a half to the east? The worries about the war in Iran, the sort of Middle East conflagration this president promised to avoid? The disappointment over the Epstein files, which failed to bring down the alleged network of deep-state pedophiles? This was not that sort of political event

No, yesterday’s Trump rally in Grand Island, Nebraska—a raspberry-colored fleck in a jammy-red state, a couple of hours from the nearest major airport—was a distinct type of Trump rally, more 2016 than 2026
It was a Midwest way station on President Trump’s recent tour of solid Republican strongholds

And it was a chance for longtime Trump supporters to show their appreciation for the two-term president who has somehow dominated the national conversation for three terms—and, more important, for him to bask in their reflected glow
Trump, after all, is in the middle of a rough stretch
Interest rates and gas prices— all prices , frankly—are high, and his approval is low
He doesn’t seem to really care how Republican candidates fare in the midterms, but he’d rather they win than lose, if only because it would save him the headache of congressional investigations

Much like his midterm convention last month in Dallas—a Trump-a-palooza that few Republicans other than Trump particularly wanted—the Nebraska rally seemed to be less about helping his party and more about reminding himself of his immovable base, via yet another trip back through the good ol’ days. (Although Nebraska’s races for governor and Senate are closer than Republicans might like, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated them “solid Republican” and “likely Republican,” respectively.) “We won this state all three times by a landslide,” Trump said, moments after taking the stage, raising the question of what exactly he was doing here

Christopher Lee for The Atlantic I have covered Trump , in some form or fashion, since early 2016, when he dispatched the candidate I had been following (Jeb!), the first of several purported giants he slayed on his way to the White House

The scene I found when I arrived in Grand Island midmorning yesterday was, in many ways, reminiscent of those early rallies, when the lines were long, the promises had not yet been broken, and Trump really might have shot people on Fifth Avenue without losing votes

Deb Reeves, a row-crop (corn, soybeans) farmer, had come to the rally with her 17-year-old grandson, Lincoln, and his buddies for the honor of seeing the president, and wanted to dispel the myth that farmers like herself are upset about the higher prices. “The farmers will take the hit because we believe that balancing the trade is going to be better for America in the long run,” the 74-year-old told me

Reeves likes Trump, she said, because “he loves this country, and I love this country.” Christopher Lee for The Atlantic Deb Reeves (center) stands with other Trump supporters ahead of the rally last night

Linda Madsen, a retired nurse, told me she likes Trump because “he’s a businessman—he’s not a politician,” and dismissed the idea that “the economy is as bad as the news people make it out.” Since her husband died, she’s been doing a lot of traveling—she recently took a Disney cruise with her granddaughter—and observed, “There’s gobs of people everywhere you go.” “People have new phones
They do everything they want to do,” said Madsen, who is 75. “So I don’t know

Is it bad, or do they just make it to be bad?” Her friend, Linda Smedra, a 78-year-old cattle rancher, said she was frustrated by Trump’s decision to allow beef imports in an attempt to drive down the cost of meat—“We ought to let the market figure out where the price needs to be”—but she agreed: “He’s done more good for the country than he’s done harm for the country.” [ Read: Trump’s secret points system for Cabinet members ] And Rose Sober told me that Trump “stands for the values America was founded on,” which she said include the Constitution, free speech, freedom, and love of the military

The 64-year-old, who doesn’t work, said that President Biden began using an autopen five days into his presidency, allowing the “Democrat socialists” to make decisions for him, and she concluded by praising Trump for surrounding himself with “God-fearing men who believe in the Bible.” “Throughout history, if you look at the Bible, God has used people like President Trump to fulfill his will,” Sober said. “There’s Daniel; there’s Joseph

I could go on.” Christopher Lee for The Atlantic Supporters of President Trump line up to attend a rally promoting Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday October 5, 2026
A disaffected Biden-Trump swing-voter crowd this was not
Even when I specifically asked attendees about the economy and inflation, they mainly blamed Biden, as Sober had, or Democrats dating as far back as Barack Obama and Bill Clinton

And in conversations with more than a dozen voters, everyone—with one notable exception—supported Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran, telling me the Islamic regime cannot get a nuclear weapon, that they’d rather fight Iran there than here, and that it was about damn time . “It’s a shame that it took us this long to handle what we should have handled,” Brennan Lavelle, a 54-year-old hog producer, told me
One woman wore a T-shirt that said, simply, Finish Iran
Yet despite the crowd’s halcyon view of the president, the Trump show last night had aspects that the man himself would not have liked

He had recently complained about what he views as the media’s unfair coverage of his crowd sizes—“The Arena was totally MAXED OUT,” he wrote on social media yesterday, after his Ohio rally—but the reality in Grand Island was similar: Yes, there was a long line that started early, snaking past nearly every building of the state fairgrounds and out along a chain-link fence on the street
But the 100,000-square-foot Pinnacle Bank Expo Center was not packed, not by a long shot, with a smattering of empty chairs and some open spaces in the back and along the sides
As the crowd filed in, premade signs of blue and red awaited them, and they were decidedly on message: No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Social Security, Lower Prices, Bigger Paychecks

The president, too, managed to accomplish the ostensible purpose of his trip; he began by touting Governor Jim Pillen, Senator Pete Ricketts, and Representative Adrian Smith, all Republicans up for reelection, and he later pulled each one onstage, allowing them to speak briefly

But he also said things that were not true, attacked the media, and strayed from the teleprompter—including when he suggested that Iran could hit a major Democratic city if the country develops a nuclear weapon. “They can take out a city,” Trump said, then seemingly shifted to imagining critics of his war displaying indifference toward that prospect: “Let them take out Los Angeles
Let them take out San Diego.” Fighting Iran, he continued, was a “very small price to pay” for avoiding such attacks
I n a parking lot before the rally began, Sany Dash peddled wares from her USA Trump Store, a potent mix of razzle-dazzle and MAGA
At political fundraisers and other private events, Dash said, she sells the sequined jackets for $250 a pop, if not more, but was offering them in Nebraska for just $100
By early afternoon, she had already sold 88

Dash, a Trump supporter who urged me not to quote her out of context, said that she has seen enthusiasm for the president fluctuate because of the war and the economy, which she noted are interconnected. “Make sure to put in that we love Trump, and we understand both sides,” she said. “We understand the wealthy, and we understand the working class
We’re in between.” After all, the Trump years have been good to Dash, who estimated that she has attended—and sold merch at—roughly 260 Trump rallies since 2016

Christopher Lee for The Atlantic The sequined jackets that Sany Dash sells at Trump rallies This particular rally was for people like Dash—or, more accurate, for Trump to be surrounded by people like Dash, those men and women who voted for him three times and would do so again if they could. (One man I spoke with fancifully suggested a Vance-Trump 2028 ticket.) The notable exception came in the form of two young men from the area, both in their early 20s and wearing black shirts that said Bibi’s favorite pawn above an image of Trump, on the front, and Good Goy on the back

The shirts, using anti-Semitic terms popular in alt-right spaces, referred to Trump’s support for Israel and, the two said, the president’s war with Iran. “We voted for Trump based on the idea of America first, right?” Creighton Mehring, an electrician, told me. “That’s what we felt that he was running for this term

And then once he got into office, we’re fighting other people’s wars.” “It’s not our war,” his friend, Dakota Van Winkle, chimed in. “Like Charlie Kirk said, it’s not our war.” [ Read: A war of assassinations ] As we stood chatting, waiting in the long line for concessions before the rally began, a black-clad security guard approached
The young men could stay, he said, they just had to keep to the back half of the room—out of view of the cameras, the president, the main crowd
The Nebraska rally was for Trump—his people, his vision of himself—and nothing would be allowed to intrude on that reality.

title: Barack Obama Looks Left
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
The Democratic Party needs Abdul El-Sayed, but it doesn’t necessarily love him
Although few top Democrats have expressed public misgivings about El-Sayed, the leftist candidate for U.S
Senate in Michigan who defeated an establishment candidate in an August primary, most of them aren’t overflowing with enthusiasm either
This hesitation is one reason yesterday’s news that former President Obama will campaign with El-Sayed and other Michigan Democrats later this month is notable

Seeing why El-Sayed would want Obama’s imprimatur is easy: He’s by far the most popular politician in America, and he won Michigan in both of his presidential races—once by more than 16 percentage points and another by nearly 10, over a native Michigander. (More unexpected is El-Sayed’s welcome for Kamala Harris, who is unpopular with leftists, lost Michigan in 2024, and has gotten a stiff arm from some Democratic candidates this cycle.) Obama’s incentives are more interesting
He is in an awkward phase of his career—no longer young enough to be cool but still too young to be an elder statesman
Nonetheless, with Bill Clinton and Joe Biden both aging and somewhat tarnished, no other figure can match Obama’s stature
He has become, as Politico put it today , the Democratic Party’s “closer-in-chief.” In that role, he’s been more willing to back left-wing candidates than other establishment figures have

Last year, many high-profile Democrats were wary of the New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani—either because they were skeptical of his policy stances or because of their long-standing ties to the family of his leading opponent, Andrew Cuomo

But Obama privately called him , praised his campaign, and offered to be a “sounding board” should Mamdani want advice. (Obama did not formally endorse Mamdani, though The New York Times , which first reported the call, noted that he prefers not to intervene in municipal races.) And in 2018, Obama endorsed Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for U.S

He did so only after she’d won a primary in a safe district, so the outcome was a foregone conclusion, but given her anti-establishment campaign, he seemed to be sending a message —or placing a bet on future success. (Obama also privately called El-Sayed after his primary victory.) Obama’s engagement with leftist candidates stands in contrast with most of his statements on leftist politics

Ideologically, Obama’s stances remain essentially center-left—even as the party overall has shifted leftward since he departed the White House —and he has at times appeared to scold or at least push back on the party’s left wing
Since leaving office, he has criticized cancel culture , slogans such as “Defund the police,” and what he views as a culture of ideological purity
Some critics on the left have been happy to return fire, labeling him a fake progressive who is too cozy with the powerful
Notwithstanding his overall popularity, Obama has drawn grumbling from other parts of the party, too
Some critics complain that he spends too much time jetting around the globe, hobnobbing with NBA stars, and podcasting with Bruce Springsteen

Even his year-end playlists and reading lists feel a bit stale. (Obama bristled when the comedian Hasan Minhaj questioned whether he really made them.) In good times, this would be merely cringe; in a time of rising authoritarianism, some view him not being more actively involved in politics as a dereliction of duty
Obama tends to lock in for campaign season, and he is a consummate party man; if the Democrats need to win the Michigan Senate seat, Obama will hit the stump for the nominee, whoever that might be
But Obama may have other reasons to embrace candidates such as El-Sayed and Mamdani
The politician who once described himself as a “skinny kid with a funny name” may see some of the same in them—or, in El-Sayed’s case, a swole kid
He is not a Muslim, as they are, but he was a target of Islamophobic attacks
And he is not a leftist, like them, but he was often tarred as a radical socialist

Beyond the personal, Obama has signaled some impatience with more traditional elements of the Democratic Party during appearances in the past two years, echoing the boisterous left more than the buttoned-up establishment

He has criticized what he sees as faintheartedness from Democrats who he said last year were “cowed and intimidated and shrinking away from just asserting what they believe, or at least what they said they believe.” In sidestepping internecine battles, he has also suggested agnosticism about methods as long as the results are good. “There’s been, I gather, some argument between the left of the party and people who are promoting the quote-unquote abundance agenda
Listen, those things are not contradictory
You want to deliver for people and make their lives better? You got to figure out how to do it,” he said

Obama will never have the same policy slate as Senator Bernie Sanders or Zohran Mamdani do, but his rhetoric and backing of leftist candidates suggest that he’s more attuned to shifts in the Democratic Party than his establishment peers are, and less rigid than his leftist critics contend
In 2008, Obama promised change; in 2026, he is still willing to give it a shot

title: ‘LOCK THE CLOCK!’
excerpt: P resident Trump is in a race against time
body: P resident Trump is in a race against time
There are 837 days left in his presidency
There are actuary tables noting the challenges of battling Father Time for 80-year-old men
But, at the moment, he is focused on one particular slice of time: daylight savings
It has become the latest obsession for a man known for not letting go of his compulsions

He has tilted against windmills, told the government to stop procuring paper straws, and spent significant mental and rhetorical energy openly discussing which is worse: electrocution in a sinking electric boat or being devoured by a shark

His attention has been pulled to daylight savings by pending legislation that would end the requirement to change clocks twice a year to match the seasons, moving an hour back in the fall and then jumping forward in the spring

Instead, he wants to keep the clock where it is after springing forward—ensuring more sunlight in the evening—and not falling back, which allows for more light in the mornings during winter months. “LOCK THE CLOCK!” the president wrote on social media over the weekend
Trump has offered a number of anecdotal arguments to support his view

During an interview with the conservative commentator Wayne Allyn Root in August, he claimed that he was once an hour late for an important meeting—“a big person from a big country”—because he had forgotten to reset his clock

He then claimed that stopping the time change would deter crime, “because criminals sleep late, you know; they do their crime in the evening.” He has suggested that it’s unsafe and costly for workers to have to reset clocks on church steeples or government buildings twice a year

He has also said that getting rid of daylight savings would lower people’s risk for cardiac issues and stroke, limit seasonal depression, and boost tourism. [ Read: A different kind of fading president ] But perhaps Trump’s most fundamental motivation became evident late last month: A president who likes to golf would like more sunlight to do so
During the final day of the Presidents Cup, held at a Chicago-area country club on September 27, Trump met with the PGA Tour Chief Executive Brian Rolapp and discussed daylight savings
A few days later, Rolapp sent Trump a letter urging him to ensure that there is more sunlight in the evenings

Too many golfers are busy with their lives and struggling to get in enough time on the course, he argued—a problem made even worse when the clocks fall back. “An extra hour of evening light sounds simple, but for everyday Americans, it can be the difference between getting on the course and not,” Rolapp wrote
The change, he said, would generate 23 million additional rounds of golf each year and pump $1 billion into the golf industry
All of this seemed to register with Trump, who operates multiple golf clubs, and who made the letter public two days later

In a midterm election in which many voters are angry about prices at the pump or in the grocery-store aisles, a closing message from the president is to stand up for the rights of golfers to get an extra hour on the green
T his particular president has known few constraints during his return to the White House
Without congressional approval, he has gone to war with Iran, torn down the East Wing, renamed large bodies of water, and closed the Kennedy Center
But Trump has not attempted to halt the changing of the clocks himself, instead conceding that he needs Congress to pass the Sunshine Protection Act
The House has passed the bill, but Trump has met resistance in the Republican-controlled Senate. “It’s dead as disco,” Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, a Republican, told Reuters last week
Trump has fixated on one particular Republican holdout: Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas

Last weekend, the president took the unusual step of posting what he claimed was the Republican’s cellphone number and urging Americans, particularly those in Arkansas, to call Cotton and demand that he vote for the bill

Cotton’s office did not respond to my requests for comment, but he has said on social media that although “no one likes changing the clock,” not doing so would mean “absurdly late sunrises” during winter months
In Fayetteville, Arkansas, the sun would rise close to 8:30 a.m. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark,” he wrote
When I tried the number that Trump posted, I was greeted by a cheery automated message: “Sorry, the mailbox is full, and there is not enough space to leave a message
Goodbye!” H istorians have traced the idea behind daylight savings back to Benjamin Franklin
In 1784, he wrote a satirical letter to the editor arguing that the government should make sure that sleep patterns coincide with the sun as a way to save money on candles
It would take more than a century for the idea to become reality: Congress enacted daylight saving time in 1918 to help conserve energy during World War I
Although Woodrow Wilson tried to keep the change permanent, Congress overrode his vetoes, and the experiment with shifting the clocks ended
But at the urging of President Franklin Roosevelt, it was reinstated in 1942 during World War II, with a new slogan: “War Time.” When the war ended, Congress again dropped the practice
In the decades afterward, some states adopted different standards, creating a confusing patchwork of time zones

William Markowitz, a time scientist at the United States Naval Observatory, at one point concluded that “the United States is the worst timekeeper in the world.” Iowa alone had 23 methods for starting and ending daylight saving time
Paul moved clocks forward for daylight savings while neighboring Minneapolis did not
Congress stepped in to create a national standard with the Uniform Time Act in 1966
Clocks would spring forward in April and fall back in October
In 1973, Congress ended the practice once again after President Richard Nixon called for the change in an address to the nation
But public support crumbled during the winter months because kids were going to school in the dark
The New York Times called it the “Second Dark Age,” and the experiment ended after less than a year

title: Trump’s Unlikely Strategy to Control History: Footnotes
excerpt: Most of Donald Trump’s efforts to control the nation’s largest museum complex have been loud
body: Most of Donald Trump’s efforts to control the nation’s largest museum complex have been loud

He tried to fire a Smithsonian museum director on social media, ordered the placement of warning signs outside its American-history museum, and demanded that the museum take down a modernist sculpture he dislikes

But while this political theater plays out publicly, the White House’s Office of Management and Budget is quietly using an obscure funding power as part of its campaign to influence how the Smithsonian tells the American story

Late last month, according to previously unreported public records, OMB included a footnote in two recent apportionments of federal funds that conditions nearly $190 million for the Smithsonian on the institution’s compliance with Trump’s March 2025 executive order accusing it of spreading “divisive narratives.” Essentially, the White House is trying to force adherence to its preferred version of history through a little-known but legally binding budget mechanism

The fiscal-year-2027 footnote, which applies to funds carried over from last year in two of the Smithsonian’s main salaries and expenses accounts, reads: To the extent permitted by law, amounts apportioned shall be available for obligation in a manner consistent with Executive Order 14253 (March 27, 2025), “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” That executive order marked the beginning of the Trump administration’s campaign to change the Smithsonian, alleging that the institution had come “under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology” and prohibiting “expenditure on exhibits or programs that degrade shared American values, divide Americans based on race, or promote programs or ideologies inconsistent with Federal law and policy.” The footnote does not specify how the Smithsonian should apply the order’s vague prohibition
But it is more than simply a threat: Apportionment footnotes are enforceable under the Antideficiency Act, the violation of which can carry criminal penalties
Such footnotes are one of several tactics that the Trump administration has used to try to supplant Congress’s spending power
In this case, the footnote suggests that the fight over the Smithsonian’s purpose goes much deeper than Trump’s most visible attacks
Today, the Smithsonian is nearly two-thirds federally funded and receives an annual total appropriation of about $1 billion—a reality that would have agonized some of its earliest supporters

In a way, John Quincy Adams could be said to have foreseen what Trump is trying to do to the Smithsonian: In 1842, the former president, then serving in Congress, opposed a bill providing federal funds to the Smithsonian, writing that the new institution in Washington, D.C., should be “exclusively confined to itself and not entangled or commingled with any national establishment requiring appropriations of public money.” Even Joseph Henry, the first Smithsonian secretary, under whom the institution began receiving regular federal funding to support a museum, worried about it, writing in an 1877 letter that the museum was “liable to be brought under direct political influence.” If there is any constant in American life, Adams and Henry knew it then and Trump knows it now: Money is control
Although the Trump administration has notched only small wins against the Smithsonian, it’s been playing money games since last year with an institution that is meant to operate independently

Starting in September of last year , OMB began adding footnotes demanding that the Smithsonian comply with two documents: the March executive order and an August letter to Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch insisting that exhibition materials and other documents be turned over for a content review

Then, starting in April of this year , the footnote was revised to require the Smithsonian to follow Trump’s budget request rather than the 2026 appropriations bill Congress had passed—essentially telling the Smithsonian to operate at a $89 million deficit from what lawmakers had legislated
After several iterations, that footnote was ultimately removed on July 2
Two days later, the White House issued a scathing report on the National Museum of American History
At that point, the footnotes tactic seemed to have gone dormant
It is unclear whether the footnotes have had any concrete impacts on the Smithsonian’s operations
The Smithsonian declined a request for an interview about the footnotes and the White House did not answer questions about the matter

Representative Chellie Pingree, a Maine Democrat who is the ranking member on the House appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Smithsonian, told me she spoke with Bunch this summer about the funding issues and got the sense that the institution was waiting to push back until the footnotes really interfered with its work
The footnotes were never challenged, she said. “I think they caused enormous heartburn for the Smithsonian

Eventually, the funds were released, and so now my worry has turned to what will happen on the next round.” Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat who is also the minority leader on a subcommittee tasked with Smithsonian oversight, condemned what he described as the refusal to release tens of millions of dollars earlier this year. “OMB used small footnotes to make a huge, absurd assertion that holding funding to the President’s budget level—just a number on a piece of paper—overrode the actual law,” he wrote to me. “In fact, it is illegal to withhold such funding.” Multiple budget experts told me these footnotes are very strange

Cerin Lindgrensavage, a lawyer at the nonpartisan watchdog group Protect Democracy, has been following apportionments closely and told me that the Smithsonian footnotes were so bespoke that a tracker that her organization had made did not flag them. “It never occurred to us that somebody would put something so egregious in text,” she said

In particular, “the idea that you would resurrect the president’s request that has zero force of law from an earlier part of the appropriations process and impose it at the very end is abhorrent to the rule of law and the constitutional order as we know it,” she said. [ Read: The next change Trump has planned for the Smithsonian ] This context makes Trump’s 2027 budget request even more ominous for the Smithsonian, because it’s the lowest for the institution in years
At $961.3 million, Trump’s proposal cuts spending by about 11 percent from the previous year

The request also stresses the importance of maintaining and protecting museums on the National Mall, which is home to about half of the Smithsonian’s museums and ground zero for Trump’s pet projects in Washington
The White House has used footnotes against other federal entities, including the National Science Foundation

Last month, a judge ruled against the Trump administration in a case about Education Department apportionments, writing that the government’s use of restrictive footnotes to force compliance with executive orders in this situation was unlawful

Remaining claims in the case, including those related to OMB using apportionments to withhold money from specific programs the administration doesn’t like, are pending. (Lindgrensavage is one of the plaintiffs’ lawyers.) Little attention has been paid to these behind-the-scenes tensions at the Smithsonian, except for when The Washington Sun reported on some of the footnotes earlier this year
The White House has justified its broader campaign by claiming that the Smithsonian presents an overly negative version of U.S. history and that its leadership has a political agenda
Historians have decried the Trump administration’s attempt to influence the institution, and Democratic lawmakers have introduced legislation to protect the Smithsonian’s independence
Smithsonian leadership has occasionally pushed back against the administration’s wider claims, saying its work is nonpartisan and rooted in scholarship
But the face-off coincides with an ongoing debate over how to tell American history

Should it be one overarching narrative or comprise many smaller, varied perspectives? Should it focus on national unity or diversity? These questions are especially top of mind at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which is widely seen as measured in its work and has followed larger curatorial and academic trends of widening the historical narrative to include more groups while emphasizing the complexities of the American story
Whatever the approach, history at the Smithsonian has been the responsibility of curators, not presidents
But the Smithsonian is in a particularly vulnerable period
Bunch will retire from his post at the end of the year

Citizen members keep dropping off the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents when their terms expire, and their seats are going unfilled, reportedly because the White House is trying to influence the new picks, The New York Time s wrote this summer

Museum-director positions are open across the institution too—last week, the director of the National Museum of Natural History announced that he is stepping down—adding to a number of major vacancies
For a president seeking control, a power vacuum and a fraying institution could represent an opportunity

One staffer who requested anonymity because she was not authorized to speak on the record told me after Bunch’s retirement announcement that some employees worried that the president might attempt to appoint a secretary, just as he “fired” National Portrait Gallery Director Kim Sajet in a Truth Social post last year. (The Smithsonian said Trump did not have the authority to do that, but she ultimately stepped down anyway). “I think you’d have to really stick your head in the sand to not feel some level of anxiety around this,” the staffer said

title: What We Really Know About the Russian ‘Plague’ Case
excerpt: In a world on edge still from the last pandemic, rumors of a deadly disease that could have escaped from a lab can cause some understandable distress—however sp
body: In a world on edge still from the last pandemic, rumors of a deadly disease that could have escaped from a lab can cause some understandable distress—however speculative they might be
Late last week, reports emerged that a woman who died in a Siberian hospital may have contracted plague, or even that she had seeded a plague outbreak

The case almost immediately set off rounds of hurried speculation within Russia and abroad; officials have shared few details, inspiring elaborate theories about what killed the woman, who worked in a plague-research facility
The fervor around the case escalated on Sunday, when Axios reported that the State Department was monitoring a “suspected plague outbreak” in Russia

So far, the evidence that the death was caused by plague or something worse is thin, in part because Russian authorities—who have a poor reputation for transparency about biosecurity—have shared few clarifications
But scientists have a good understanding of how plague works
And if the lab worker did contract plague, that is no cause for international panic

Sometime in the past week, a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, not far from the Mongolian border, died of “pneumonia of an unknown cause,” Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s agency for consumer protection and public health, said Sunday
Government officials have not confirmed her identity, but Russian media have reported that the woman was Daria Shipilova, a 27- or 28-year-old technician at the lab
A local official said that the hospital where she was treated has been placed under quarantine; local media, meanwhile, reported that several hospitals were under quarantine

And Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement on Friday that other people—local media later reported the number as 200—may have been in contact with a resident who contracted an “especially dangerous infection,” and were placed under medical observation
He did not identify the resident as Shipilova or say that the person had died

The public-health agency told state media that “no micro-organisms linked to her professional activity were identified in the patient’s samples” and that no contacts have experienced “health changes related to infectious pathology.” Meanwhile, an aluminum factory in the same town as the laboratory imposed a mask mandate for its more than 2,000 employees, The Wall Street Journal reported
Plague might sound medieval, but it’s endemic among animals in many parts of the world today
Although Russia hasn’t reported any plague cases to the WHO since at least 2018, Mongolia has
An average of seven cases are recorded in the United States every year, typically from a flea bite or handling infected animals
More than 80 percent of U.S. cases are the bubonic form of the disease, which presents with swollen, pus-filled lymph nodes
Two other main forms of plague, all caused by the same bacterium, are also occasionally reported around the world: septicemic, which infects the blood, and pneumonic, which infects the lungs
Because the lab worker died of pneumonia, speculation that she’d died from plague centered on this last form
Pneumonic plague is the sole form of the disease that can transmit between humans, but that doesn’t mean it’s particularly likely to spread

David Wagner, the executive director of Northern Arizona University’s Pathogen and Microbiome Institute, told me that the respiratory droplets that can spread pneumonic plague—not to be confused with the tinier aerosols that can spread diseases such as flu and COVID—are only released during a cough or sneeze and only travel about three to six feet. “You have to be in very close proximity to someone with pneumonic plague to contract it from them,” he said

Because transmission between humans is relatively difficult, the Russian government’s response to the mystery death from pneumonia—placing 200 people under medical observation—is “really incongruent with what you would expect for plague,” Amesh Adalja, an infectious-disease physician at Johns Hopkins University, told me

Daniel Jernigan, the former director of the CDC’s National Center for Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases, told me that response was “above and beyond” what is typically required for plague cases

Perhaps, he said, the Russian authorities acted out of an abundance of caution; per Reuters , a local official recently said that most of the hospital workers who had been placed under quarantine have already been released
Even if Shipilova did die of plague, fears of a larger outbreak are probably moot by now
Plague has an incubation period of only one to seven days, so anyone Shipilova might have exposed would have come down with symptoms by now, Jernigan said
Russian authorities have said that no one under medical observation has tested positive for plague

Generally speaking, the chances of a large outbreak of plague are slim. “Once you have an accurate diagnosis, it’s readily treated with multiple types of antibiotics, which is why we don’t have massive plague outbreaks and pandemics anymore,” Wagner said

Very quickly, though, some scientists, security experts, and media outlets began speculating that whatever killed Shipilova was not traditional pneumonic plague, but a dangerous pathogen that had been somehow altered in the lab
The fear is that the pathogen could be resistant to antibiotics or other treatments, making it harder to prevent an outbreak
No evidence so far suggests that’s true or that the Irkutsk lab was modifying plague bacteria to make it more dangerous

Still, the host of unanswered questions surrounding this case has paved the way for conjectures about links to biological weapons and for conspiracy thinking about government collusion and vaccine companies set to profit off a plague pandemic

Some Russian media outlets reported—and international outlets repeated—that the woman contracted plague after she broke a test tube containing a sample of the disease. (If that was the case, Adalja said, the lab should have followed the standard procedure of prescribing antibiotics immediately after exposure, which has not been reported.) And in the past, the Russian government has worked on bioterrorist agents and hidden the true cause of disease outbreaks
For example, Soviet officials attributed a 1979 anthrax outbreak that killed at least 64 people to contaminated meat
More than a decade later, President Boris Yeltsin admitted that the anthrax had come from a military biological-weapons facility
The war in Ukraine has increased speculation about planned biological threats

In 2022, the Russian military began refurbishing a Soviet-era laboratory to handle deadly pathogens such as Ebola viruses, The Washington Post reported. “There’s just a standard lack of transparency from the Russian government that adds to the vacuum of information,” Adalja said
The U.S. government, for its part, has given inconsistent signals about whether it believes that the incident has wider implications
Along with the State Department, the CDC and the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response are reportedly working to learn more about the death

But Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplayed the possibility of danger to reporters yesterday, saying, “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it.” Today, he called on Russia to be more transparent and share more information

title: Homme Fatale
excerpt: At a dive bar deep in coal country, Derek Zoolander, male model, sits with his father and brothers after they’ve spent a long day in the mines
body: At a dive bar deep in coal country, Derek Zoolander, male model, sits with his father and brothers after they’ve spent a long day in the mines
An ad for the beauty company Aveda comes on the TV—a spot that, as luck would have it, features Derek at his male-modeliest: hair gelled, torso nude, skin shimmering with body glitter

He also has a tail, a fishy pastel-green appendage that has been grafted onto his lower extremities via a protean form of CGI. “Moisture is the essence of wetness,” the ad’s narrator intones, as Derek (played by Ben Stiller) flaps around in an unconvincing ocean. “And wetness is the essence of beauty.” Surf and turf, but make it fashion : The joke pretty much delivers itself
But it also functions, in Zoolander , as a plot device
As the ad plays, Derek seems thrilled: Finally, his family will see him

Derek’s father (a steely Jon Voight) professes his relief that his wife, having died, never had to “see her son as a mermaid.” The line is harsh—it might be the most piercing in the film—but if there’s one thing viewers learn about Derek Zoolander, it’s that he will, like a phoenix with a fish tail, persevere

Out of the awkward silence, inspirational music begins to swell. “Mer- man ,” Derek corrects his father, the music growing louder around him. “Mer- MAN !” If Zoolander is a bit like its namesake—absurdly farcical, endlessly watchable—Stiller’s chimeric turn helps explain why

When the film premiered 25 years ago, it had everything: an all-star cast (Owen Wilson as Derek’s nemesis, Hansel; Will Ferrell as the arch-villain; David Duchovny as the most celebrated hand model of all time), a gonzo plot (male models brainwashed to serve as assassins!), and a warm human heart
It debuted in theaters in late September of 2001

Its early earnings, in that grim moment, were tepid, its reviews decidedly bad. (Roger Ebert, so often a champion of cinematic absurdity, met Derek’s assorted contortions with a signature pose of his own: a thumb turned emphatically down .) But Zoolander , in the years afterward, gradually ascended to filmdom’s version of haute couture: It became a cult classic, beloved for both its ostentatious idiocy and its insistence that dim-wittedness, seen from the right angle, can be wise

Today—with its hero’s insistence that he can vamp to the camera, covered in body glitter, and still be a (mer)man—it looks downright prescient. [ Adam Serwer: The masculinity scam ] Zoolander arrived on the scene as the gender swap, that old cinematic trope, was losing its last traces of subversion
The film did not, on its face, deploy the gimmick; Derek is no Tootsie and certainly no Mrs
As a model, he is a man doing work traditionally done by a woman—a guy whose job is to be gazed at and otherwise lucratively objectified
As a male model, though, he is doing a version of what his father and brothers do every day in the coal mines: asserting, and then typifying, an extremely legible version of manliness
The gender-bending is in one way Zoolander ’s most basic joke
Derek takes an insult traditionally lobbed at women— bimbo —and twists it around into a cherished and revealing archetype: the himbo
The bimbo, from her earliest days, was most directly an answer to the vixen and the femme fatale
She enticed, yes, but she never threatened
She may have been voluptuous (she almost definitely was) but she was also fundamentally flat
The bimbo’s vacuity functions as an invitation, effectively, to the people who see her: Go ahead and look
It turns a three-dimensional person into a two-dimensional image and then, in an elegant little trick, insists that she, herself, is responsible for the flattening
The bimbo is silly and empty and treated accordingly
Why consider the person behind the appearance when, the stereotype insists, there is none? The himbo operates similarly
His attractiveness—his never-misses-leg-day show of masculinity—is his blessing and his curse
It elevates him as someone to be looked at, and it demeans him as some thing to be looked at
He is demeaned in terms usually reserved for women
He is a male model caught in the male gaze
Gender swapping can be a gimmick, but it can also offer insights
And as Derek tries bimbohood on for size, he demonstrates how silly the idea has always been
It is one of the primary sources of his appeal
Derek is not, on the face of things, an obvious hero
He can be superficial (learning that his love interest was heavy in her youth, he responds with a knee-jerk “ew”)
He can be vain (at the VH1 Fashion Awards, unable to fathom not being named Male Model of the Year, he barrels to the stage, so self-absorbed that he didn’t hear Hansel’s name being called)

He is the kind of guy who will wear white to a funeral and use the eulogy as an opportunity to talk about himself—and then insist that eulogy is pronounced “you- goog -ly.” But his himbohood redeems him
It is what allows him to work as Zoolander ’s protagonist—and to be seen, in his lighthearted way, as worthy of celebration
A himbo’s charm lies in the discrepancy between what he might be and what he is: Big and burly, he could treat manliness as something to be wielded
But he is too gentle for that, too dim-witted, too pure
He is a hold-harmless clause in human form
And Derek, being exceptionally burly and exceptionally dim, is more reassuring than most
Even when he is brainwashed into violence, he is incapable of carrying it out

title: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers
excerpt: Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds
body: Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds

Drug giants Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their drugs age less quickly, according to readouts from molecular “aging clocks.” Such clocks assess a person’s biological age by looking at changes to DNA that accumulate with time, or, in newer versions, by tracking levels of key proteins

Both companies found that overweight or diabetic patients taking the drugs, called GLP-1s, had reduced biological age compared to those taking a placebo, although the difference varied widely, depending on which type of clock was used, and what organ was tested.  Overall, the difference was around “two to three years,” according to Nikolaj Roed, a global project leader at Novo, who says the company has been seeing “improved biological age in our patients across trials and across different tissues.”  The findings add to wide speculation among scientists that GLP-1 drugs, as they are known, are acting on basic causes of aging and might be a true longevity treatment. “Two years is a pretty strong effect, in my book,” says Steve Horvath, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who’s credited with inventing aging clocks

Horvath says the emerging data could provide “evidence that these GLP-1 drugs are actually what is known as geroprotectors, medications that slow or possibly even reverse biologic aging.” The companies shared their findings over the weekend during Aging Research & Drug Discovery, a conference devoted to seeking scientific remedies for old age

While that quest has not yet produced any clear-cut success, some scientists now think Novo’s drug semaglutide (sold under the names Ozempic and Wegovy) is coming close. “In an unhealthy population, I do think it’s an anti-aging drug,” says Vadim Gladyshev, a Harvard biologist who assisted Novo with its molecular measurements. “But in a healthy population, no one knows.” The drugs cause weight loss by stimulating a receptor, GLP-1, that tells your brain you’re not hungry
Yet real-world studies have shown much wider benefit

The drugs improve kidney function, reduce blood pressure, and even sharply cut the overall chance of death. “If the question is,‘Can semaglutide reach several diseases relevant to health span and aging?’ we know we can say the answer is yes,” said Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, a senior scientific director at Novo, the Danish drug giant, during the meeting

The next question to answer, he said, is whether such effects are accompanied by changes to molecular measures of biological aging: “When you intervene with semaglutide, does it actually move the clocks in any direction? And the answer is yes.”  The company found that, over time, the drugs cause a wide slowdown in aging clocks—as much as 4 years in the case of a clock that looks at heart proteins. “I think it’s pretty clear that the organ age is shifting,” said Aguayo-Orozco
The studies are also a huge boost for the science of aging clocks
Although these measures reflect a person’s age, it’s been uncertain if they are useful as true biomarkers

Now clock makers have evidence  that their readouts show a drop in age when people take drugs with broad, well-demonstrated benefits.   “The clock people have been pushing for a decade to get this kind of study done,” says Yuge Ji, a biologist who previously worked in the field and now runs a startup, Reflector Bio. “It’s huge for them.” As part of its study, Novo took blood draws from 10,052 people, half on the drug and half on a placebo

Their blood, collected at the start of the study as well as months later, was then measured with “proteomic clocks,” which use levels of key proteins to predict a person’s age and risk of dying .  Scientists at Eli Lilly performed similar research on their GLP-1 drug, tirzepatide, using so-called “epigenetic” clocks that assess age by counting accumulated changes to DNA

Lilly’s study was smaller, but also found that for the most part, molecular time moved more slowly for people on the drug.   “All the clocks are telling a consistent story that we’re seeing a reduction in age,” Kevin Duffin, vice president for aging research at Lilly, said during the conference. “It’s not like we’re going to reverse age by 30 years or something, but it’s a significant reduction.” The molecules have become the best selling drugs in the world,, with Lilly’s tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro for diabetes and Zepbound for obesity, topping the list with more than $36 billion in revenue to the company last year
Novo’s semaglutide, also sold under more than one name, was a close second

Alex Zhavoronkov, the founder of Insilico Medicine, and the organizer of the Boston meeting, says that extending lives by even one year across the world’s population would be equal to tens of millions of lifetimes.   Last month Zhavoronkov showed that one of his company’s drugs, for a lung disease, also reversed the signals from aging clocks
That drug is experimental, but Zhavoronkov has sought to promote the idea that humanity is entering a new era of longevity medicines

He also disclosed during the event that he has been “microdosing” the available weight-loss drugs, even though he is not overweight. “I am on tirzepatide and I am an equal-opportunity injector of semaglutide as well,” Zhavoronkov said

It was part of an effort to directly raise the question of whether the first mass-market anti-aging remedy is already here. “Do you think a reasonable person should start taking semaglutide?” he asked Aguayo-Orozco, the Novo scientist, in front of a crowded audience. “I am not a physician
I cannot answer that question,” Aguayo-Orozco replied
Several people cautioned that GLP-1 drugs do have side effects, including muscle loss

That is one reason they might not help most people, says Horvath, who says he isn’t ready to take the drugs himself, although he’s thought about it. “Clearly, the drugs have many benefits in obese people, but I did not yet see sufficient evidence that they will benefit skinny people,” he said. “I guess we will have to wait.” Answers could start to emerge in a year or two
This past January, a US agency, ARPA-H, put $38 million toward a study in Texas that will attempt to determine whether semaglutide has anti-aging effects in healthy people over 60
That research will look at changes in cognition, mobility, and acuity of the senses
That project also seeks to help define a regulatory pathway for anti-aging drugs and to “build a new therapeutic industry” around longevity.

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. 10 climate tech companies to watch Each year, MIT Technology Review puts together a list of the most promising climate tech companies in the world
This year, the stakes feel higher than ever

The world is on track for one of its hottest years on record, climate-fueled disasters are taking lives and costing billions, while political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress.  We urgently need to cut emissions and avoid climate change’s most harmful effects, and that’s where our 10 companies come in.  They’re working on everything from mobile flood barriers and semi-solid-state batteries to compressed-CO₂ energy storage and next-generation nuclear reactors
They also reflect the biggest shifts in climate tech—including the surging energy demands of AI data centers.  Meet the 10 companies working on some of the biggest challenges in climate tech

title: Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
excerpt: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge fe
body: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.  This year is shaping up to be one of the hottest ever recorded
The world must begin to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions to address the climate crisis, which is already affecting communities around the globe
Wildfires, floods, and other climate-fueled disasters are killing thousands and costing billions of dollars
At the same time, political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress, particularly in the US.  Technology alone can’t solve climate change

But we believe innovations can help us make real changes and improve lives around the world as we try to address one of the most pressing challenges of our time.  In this project, we look for companies developing technologies that can help us face the climate crisis

Some are driving down the greenhouse-gas emissions fueling climate change; others are working to reduce the dangers that communities face from extreme heat, drought, or other shifts brought on by a warming planet

We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.  When we set out to build our list, we start by soliciting nominations from our team of reporters and editors
We ask experts for suggestions and reach out to academics, researchers, investors, and analysts

Once we have a pool of nominees, we then consider each one, digging through literature, reports, and patents to vet both the technology and the business.  We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall
We want the final slate of companies to represent a range of industries and include firms based around the globe that are at different stages of development
We also aim to strike a balance between highlighting companies previously included and introducing new names
Finally, we consider some of the most important trends and events of the year and look for nominees that reflect those developments
The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech
Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US
China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate

This year’s list includes two Chinese companies: WeLion is building semi-solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, and Envision Energy is installing huge amounts of wind power and energy storage in China and around the world.  Several sectors stood out this year as being of particular importance

One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.  Energy storage is a key piece of that puzzle because it can smooth out variations in the electricity supply as grids incorporate more renewable power
We’ve included several energy storage companies on this year’s list
Energy Dome is building long-duration energy storage systems on the grid that rely on compressed carbon dioxide
Moment Energy is a Canadian company working to repurpose EV batteries for grid-scale storage

And Form Energy , which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.  A wide range of technologies is represented here: everything from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors

Some of the awardees might be familiar from our past coverage; others are just emerging and may be less well known.  We believe we’ve put together a list filled with businesses that are rising to the challenge of this moment
Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount
By helping us make progress on tackling the climate crisis in such difficult times, these companies point to a better way forward.

title: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries
excerpt: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries
body: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries
The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones

From the EVs that carry commuters home to the ships that transport goods across countries, more and more vehicles around us are powered by batteries.  Lithium-ion batteries are commonly used to power personal devices and vehicles today
But as the need for batteries surges, there’s a growing appetite for cells that can store more energy on a single charge

Also, in lithium-based batteries the electrolyte, which facilitates ion transfer, uses a flammable liquid that can create a fire hazard.  Several companies, including WeLion New Energy, are working to make solid-state cells, which use a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one
This could increase the energy density of batteries, as well as improve their safety
Fully solid-state cells are extremely difficult to manufacture, though
So WeLion currently focuses on developing and producing semi-solid-state cells, which have a part-liquid, part-solid electrolyte.  On that front, they have made steady progress
In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack in partnership with Shanghai-based EV-maker Nio, best known for its battery-swapping technology
The pack had an energy density of 360 watt-hours per kilogram (wh/kg), significantly higher than the 200 wh/kg average for lithium-ion packs today
That translated to a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles)

However, only about 200 of the battery packs were manufactured due to their high production cost, but they are still being used by Nio, WeLion says.  WeLion has also built batteries to power cargo ships and ferries through a subsidiary
And the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density too

WeLion’s engineers made a semi-solid-state battery that achieved a remarkable energy density of 824 wh/kg during testing in 2025, more than three times that of a standard lithium-ion battery available today.  Key indicators Industry: Energy storage Founded: 2016 Headquarters: Beijing, China Notable fact: WeLion’s cofounders include Chen Liquan, a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who led the development of the country’s first all-solid-state battery back in 1988
Potential for impact China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country, and its transportation sector accounts for around 10% of that total

Scaling up the production of safer, higher-capacity batteries could help switch more vehicles away from fossil fuels.  Batteries that power electric ships could be especially helpful—the carbon dioxide emissions from vessels that move goods along China’s lakes, canals, and rivers are projected to grow by around 25% in this decade alone, reaching 18.7 million metric tons by 2030.  Caveats   One big challenge WeLion faces is scaling up production of its semi-solid-state batteries and competing on cost in a crowded battery market

WeLion says that its semi-solid-state batteries are more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries made by larger Chinese battery companies such as CATL.  And while laboratory tests showing high energy density are impressive, it can be difficult to translate laboratory results to the real world
The company declined to give more details about the experimental results from its 2025 prototype, which it says is far from commercialization

Key details remain unclear, including how many times the cell can be charged and discharged and how capacity degrades over its lifetime.   Next steps  WeLion plans to bring a new semi-solid-state battery for drones to market with an energy density of 410 wh/kg by the end of this year

It also intends to introduce its first all-solid-state battery for cars in 2027, which is expected to have an energy density of 400 wh/kg.  Two inland cargo ships powered by WeLion’s batteries are expected to launch in October 2026 in Huzhou, a city in eastern China
The battery pack of each of these ships will be able to carry nearly 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough for them to sail for up to 250 kilometers (155 miles), the company says
Today, WeLion has an annual manufacturing capacity of 11 gigawatt-hours (GWh) spread between four production bases in China
Two additional plants with a combined yearly capacity of 18 GWh are under construction.

title: Form Energy and its iron batteries
excerpt: Form Energy is building iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days
body: Form Energy is building iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days
The company is ramping up supply at its factory and signing deals for commercial projects
New solar and wind installations produce electricity more affordably than fossil fuels in most places, but their output varies based on season, time of day, and weather

To compensate, utilities are increasingly investing in battery storage systems, which can charge when power is abundant and discharge when the grid needs a boost.  Lithium-ion batteries are the fastest-growing storage technology

Although light and energy-dense, they require pricey metals and are costly to scale, and few of the large batteries of this type used in industry are designed to store energy for longer than four to six hours
Form Energy wants to build cheaper long-duration energy storage technology
The company has developed a new type of battery, built with a far more abundant and cheaper metal, iron, that can store energy for 100 hours
It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting.” During discharge, oxygen from the air converts the iron metal to rust, releasing electrons
When charging, current converts the rust back into iron metal.  Over the past two years, Form has gained commercial traction

It began producing batteries at its West Virginia factory for its first commercial deployment, a 150 megawatt-hour system for Minnesota electricity provider Great River Energy, which is set to come online in 2027
And Form has signed several other deals with power providers
The largest is a project with another Minnesota-based utility, Xcel Energy, where wind and solar power, backed by 30 gigawatt-hours of Form’s batteries, will be used to power a new Google data center
That project is expected to come online in phases between 2028 and 2031

Key indicators Industry: Energy storage Founded: 2017 Headquarters: Somerville, Massachusetts, US Notable fact: Once complete, Form’s proposed 30 gigawatt-hour energy storage system at a Google data center in Minnesota could be the world’s largest battery project by energy capacity
Potential for impact Wind and solar power play a major role in limiting growth in global carbon dioxide emissions
Still, many grid operators depend on fossil fuel plants, especially natural gas ones, to fill gaps caused by periods of low renewable supply or high demand
Form’s batteries are designed to cover multiday supply-demand imbalances, like those that crop up during heat waves, deep freezes, or periods with little sun or wind
The company declined to share the current cost of its battery systems, but says its goal is to reach $20 per kilowatt-hour, which would make them cost-competitive with the natural gas alternative
The company’s technology could help reduce emissions from the AI data center boom
AI’s thirst for energy has already delayed closure of aging coal plants , led to the building of new natural gas plants, and caused price hikes for consumers
Cheap energy storage could help renewables meet more of this AI-driven growth in electricity demand.  FORM ENERGY Caveats The long-duration storage market is still nascent
Form’s iron-air technology faces a crowded field of approaches, including pumped hydropower, compressed gas, fuel cells, gravitational devices, and flow batteries that store energy in liquids

The economics of multiday batteries, which require large capital expenditures yet frequently sit idle, remain tricky.   While funding from data center developers could be a major boost, Form also has to prove it can deliver: Its existing production capacity, 2 gigawatt-hours of battery storage per year, is a fraction of the 80 gigawatt-hours it has promised through commercial agreements
Success will hinge on its ability to scale
Another remaining question is the technology’s physical footprint
Form’s batteries, which are stacked together in enclosures the size of shipping containers, require an acre for every two to three megawatts

That means its Google installation would take up the equivalent of at least 75 football fields.   Next steps In addition to finalizing its first commercial project, Form is outfitting its factory with new equipment that will help it scale manufacturing to meet its production backlog
It will do so with the help of new financing, announced in August, that brings its total money raised, in addition to West Virginia state and US federal grants, to more than $2 billion.

title: I’m a physicist who worked on the Nobel-winning neutrino search – here’s how a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice became a telescope for ghost particles from space
url:
<title>I’m a physicist who worked on the Nobel-winning neutrino search – here’s how a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice became a telescope for ghost particles from space</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764306/original/file-20261006-60-ds0ckd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=486%2C308%2C6187%2C4124&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The IceCube observatory sits atop the South Pole&#39;s 1.8-miles-thick pure, clear ice sheet.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/gallery/the-icecube-upgrade/#modulagallery-22914-22968">Ilya Bodo, IceCube/NSF</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Standing at the South Pole is the next-best thing to being on another planet. If you walk a few hundred yards away from the National Science Foundation’s <a href="https://www.nsf.gov/news/special_reports/livingsouthpole/intro.jsp">research station</a>, you see a featureless plain of snow and ice, most likely empty of living creatures larger than microbes for hundreds of miles.</p>

<p>With nothing but snow for sound waves to echo off, there’s an eerie silence. It’s easy to get lost in reverie, contemplating the stark landscape. But then I remember that I’m here for a reason: to work on what may be the world’s weirdest telescope, watching for some of nature’s most mysterious subatomic particles.</p>

<p>This wintry landscape is home to the <a href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/">IceCube Neutrino Observatory</a>. This unusual telescope is the brainchild of <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=tTNPXRsAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Francis Halzen</a>, recipient of the <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2026/press-release/">2026 Nobel Prize in physics</a> for his work spearheading this project and discovering high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.</p>

<p><a href="https://inspirehep.net/authors/1011886">I’m an astrophysicist</a> and part of the international team of scientists who started building IceCube in 2005 and continue to operate it today. Although the detector is designed to be operated mostly remotely, some work must be done in person: maintaining and replacing electronics, installing new hardware and upgrading instruments.</p>

<p>Every student and scientist who comes to the South Pole feels that same sense of awe. Even when we’re analyzing data back in our offices at home, images from our time at the pole lurk in the back of our minds.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Bundled up construction workers with metal beams on snowy landscape." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=564&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=564&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101731/original/image-20151112-9381-3cnoxx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=564&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Neutrinos hint at where cosmic rays come from</h2>

<p>Every second, more than <a href="https://pdg.lbl.gov/2026/reviews/rpp2026-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf">10,000 high-energy particles</a> – protons and atomic nuclei – rain down from space on every square meter of the Earth’s atmosphere. Some of them carry more than a million times the energy of the protons at the most powerful particle accelerator, the <a href="https://home.cern/science/accelerators/large-hadron-collider/">Large Hadron Collider</a> at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research. Fortunately, the atmosphere absorbs most of them, but a few stray particles pass through your body every second.</p>

<p>Scientists discovered these particles, known as cosmic rays, more than a century ago.</p>

<p>But the magnetic fields that fill the universe deflect cosmic rays on their journey, so the direction they’re traveling when they reach Earth’s surface doesn’t tell us where they were originally produced.  </p>

<p>Since the cosmic rays themselves don’t point back to their sources, we look instead for neutrinos, a type of subatomic particle that should be produced as a byproduct of cosmic ray acceleration, wherever it’s happening. </p>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/how-neutrinos-which-barely-exist-just-ran-off-with-another-nobel-prize-48726">Neutrinos are very strange</a> – they’ve been called ghost particles. They very rarely interact with other matter, so to see them, you need a very large detector. Our telescope is called <a href="http://icecube.wisc.edu">IceCube</a> because we use a cubic kilometer – a billion tons – of the Antarctic ice cap to catch neutrinos.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A tether descends into a vertical tunnel through snowy ice." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=800&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101746/original/image-20151112-9366-17htjfm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1005&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">One of IceCube’s 91 strings of sensors, called DOMs (digital optical modules), is lowered into the ice. They’re vertically spaced about 55 feet (17 meters) apart and meant to catch the visual repercussions of a neutrino collision.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="http://icecube.wisc.edu/gallery/press/view/1336">Jim Haugen, IceCube/NSF</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/">CC BY-NC</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Most neutrinos pass invisibly through IceCube, but by chance a few of them will smash into a proton or neutron in the ice, releasing a shower of high-energy electrons, photons and other particles the detectors can see. By measuring the number and direction of these visible particles, we can determine the direction the original neutrino came from, its energy and its type, also called its “<a href="https://neutrinos.fnal.gov/types/flavor/">flavor</a>.” One by one, we build up a picture of the sky as it shines in neutrinos, rather than starlight.</p>

<p>Halzen proposed the idea of building a neutrino telescope in Antarctica in 1988. The South Pole may not sound like the obvious place to build such a telescope, but in fact it’s the easiest place to do it. The United States maintains a <a href="https://www.nsf.gov/od/opp/ail/amundson-scott-south-pole-station">scientific facility there</a>, home to several other experiments besides IceCube.</p>

<p>Most importantly for us, the South Pole station sits on top of nearly 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) of the purest, clearest ice in the world – a perfect neutrino target just waiting to be used.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People in winter gear cluster around an airplane on snowy ground." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/101729/original/image-20151112-9385-s93ygo.JPG?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
