              <span class="caption">Planes need skis to land and take off at the South Pole.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="http://icecube.wisc.edu/gallery/view/211">Mark Krasberg, IceCube/NSF</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/">CC BY-NC</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Good for science, tough for people</h2>

<p>But “easiest” is not the same as “easy” – the South Pole is a challenging place to work. Traveling to the pole from the U.S. usually takes a week or more. The last leg of the trip is on a special ski-equipped LC-130 cargo aircraft, operated by the Air National Guard, which lands on a runway made of compressed snow.</p>

<p>These aircraft can only reach the pole for four months of the year: at midsummer – January in the Southern Hemisphere – the average temperature is a balmy minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 26 degrees Celsius), but by March, temperatures have fallen to minus 50 F (minus 45 C), too cold for LC-130s to operate.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two people sit in beach chairs on snow clinking bottles with the sun coming over horizon." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=574&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=721&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=721&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764326/original/file-20261006-50-n0owwf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=721&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Two ‘winter-overs’ toast the return of the Sun.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/gallery/winterovers/#modulagallery-3160-2167">Martin Wolf, IceCube/NSF</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>We pack our work into those summer months, then hand IceCube off to two hardy “winter-over” scientists. Our winter-overs are part of a team of 45 people who <a href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/pole/daily-life/">stay at the station</a> for the rest of the year, cut off from the rest of the world for eight months except for internet and radio communications.</p>

<p>In the summer, the station population expands to around 150 people. The South Pole is a high-altitude desert, so the air is thin and very, very dry. But the cold isn’t the toughest part of working at the South Pole – at least in the summer. The strangest thing, at least for me, is the constant daylight.</p>

<p>At the South Pole, the <a href="https://www.antarctica.gov.au/about-antarctica/weather-and-climate/weather/sunlight-hours/">Sun stays up for six months</a>, circling along the horizon and slowly spiraling down until it sets at the autumn equinox. Then our winter-overs get six months of constant darkness until sunrise in the spring. This plays havoc with circadian rhythms; I’ve awoken to see the clock read 3:00, not knowing whether it’s a.m. or p.m., whether I’ve slept for four hours or 16.</p>

<p>Despite being one of the most isolated places on Earth, the station is also very crowded in the summer. It takes a lot of expensive fuel to heat the buildings, so space is at a premium – and needless to say, most of us work indoors. It also takes fuel to melt water, so showers are rationed to two minutes of running water twice a week, contributing to the unique working atmosphere at the South Pole. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Blue dotted lines descend through a black background in an artist's rendering." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764323/original/file-20261006-50-6nu9hi.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An illustration shows how when a neutrino interacts in the clear Antarctic ice, it produces secondary particles that leave a trace of blue light as they travel through the IceCube detector.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/gallery/high-energy-neutrinos-from-the-galactic-plane/#modulagallery-10913-1770">Nicolle R. Fuller/NSF/IceCube</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Results rolled in</h2>

<p>The road to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory was a long one. Halzen started work at the South Pole in 1993 with a project called AMANDA, which I joined in 1997. AMANDA showed we could <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/35068509">detect neutrinos in the ice</a>, but it was too small to see any sources – it was like using binoculars when what we needed was a serious telescope.</p>

<p>We needed to go big. Halzen built a team that could scale up the process and convinced scientific agencies in the U.S. and other countries that the results would be worthwhile. IceCube was fully commissioned in 2011, on schedule and on budget, with Halzen coordinating the efforts of over 300 scientists around the world.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/3PZgfPHULHw?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A neutrino interacting with the ice inside the IceCube telescope produces electrically charged secondary particles that are detected thanks to a process called Cherenkov radiation. The Cherenkov light, a blue light emitted by charged particles passing through a medium at a speed greater than the speed of light in that medium, will spread through the ice over hundreds of meters.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Two years after IceCube was completed, we announced that we’d identified <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1242856">neutrinos from outside the solar system</a> – the original entries in our map of the neutrino sky. We named the first two Bert and Ernie.</p>

<p>By now, we’ve seen thousands of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1103/2gh9-d4q7">neutrinos coming from the cosmos</a>, some with hundreds of times more energy than the protons accelerated at CERN. But it’s been surprisingly difficult to determine where, exactly, they come from. No individual sources immediately stand out in the sky – most of the neutrinos form a diffuse glow, like seeing sky glow at night rather than distinct constellations of stars.</p>

<p>IceCube is making progress pinpointing the origins of some of the cosmic rays by identifying their neutrino emission. One high-energy neutrino <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aat1378">came from a blazar</a> – a supermassive black hole sucking in matter from its host galaxy and spewing some of it into a jet thousands of light-years long and pointed straight at Earth. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg3395">Others came</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/addd05">from nearby</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ae4aad">galaxies</a> and a few even <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adc9818">from our own Milky Way</a>.</p>

<p>But these sources can only account for <a href="https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ae4aac">a small fraction of the neutrinos IceCube detects</a>. Many questions remain, and more work is needed to answer them.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A built structure against blue sky and snowy ground as far as visible." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764394/original/file-20261006-50-luk6iv.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">The IceCube Upgrade hardware will fine-tune the neutrino data and help researchers find more neutrino sources.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">E. Krupczak/NSF-IceCube</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the 2025-26 South Pole summer, we installed the <a href="https://icecube.wisc.edu/news/press-releases/2026/02/the-icecube-neutrino-observatory-gets-a-major-upgrade-beneath-the-ice/">IceCube Upgrade</a>, an extension designed to bring the sky into sharper focus by improving the detector’s calibration. Plans for another, even larger <a href="https://icecube-gen2.wisc.edu">IceCube Gen2</a> Observatory are under development, and there are a handful of other neutrino telescopes under construction around the world, including <a href="https://www.km3net.org/">KM3NeT</a>, <a href="https://baikalgvd.jinr.ru/">Baikal-GVD</a>, <a href="https://trident.sjtu.edu.cn/en">TRIDENT</a>, and a new project I’m working on called <a href="https://www.pacific-neutrino.org/">P-ONE</a>.</p>

<p>IceCube has given us our first peek behind the curtain at the most powerful neutrino sources in the universe, and I’m excited to see what other surprises are in store.</p>

body: The IceCube observatory sits atop the South Pole's 1.8-miles-thick pure, clear ice sheet
Ilya Bodo, IceCube/NSF Standing at the South Pole is the next-best thing to being on another planet

If you walk a few hundred yards away from the National Science Foundation’s research station , you see a featureless plain of snow and ice, most likely empty of living creatures larger than microbes for hundreds of miles
With nothing but snow for sound waves to echo off, there’s an eerie silence
It’s easy to get lost in reverie, contemplating the stark landscape
But then I remember that I’m here for a reason: to work on what may be the world’s weirdest telescope, watching for some of nature’s most mysterious subatomic particles
This wintry landscape is home to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory

This unusual telescope is the brainchild of Francis Halzen , recipient of the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics for his work spearheading this project and discovering high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin
I’m an astrophysicist and part of the international team of scientists who started building IceCube in 2005 and continue to operate it today
Although the detector is designed to be operated mostly remotely, some work must be done in person: maintaining and replacing electronics, installing new hardware and upgrading instruments
Every student and scientist who comes to the South Pole feels that same sense of awe
Even when we’re analyzing data back in our offices at home, images from our time at the pole lurk in the back of our minds
Workers construct the support tower for the hot water ‘drill’ used to melt holes 1.5 miles (2.4 kilometers) deep in the Antarctic ice to install IceCube sensors

Jeff Cherwinka, IceCube/NSF , CC BY-NC Neutrinos hint at where cosmic rays come from Every second, more than 10,000 high-energy particles – protons and atomic nuclei – rain down from space on every square meter of the Earth’s atmosphere
Some of them carry more than a million times the energy of the protons at the most powerful particle accelerator, the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research
Fortunately, the atmosphere absorbs most of them, but a few stray particles pass through your body every second
Scientists discovered these particles, known as cosmic rays, more than a century ago

But the magnetic fields that fill the universe deflect cosmic rays on their journey, so the direction they’re traveling when they reach Earth’s surface doesn’t tell us where they were originally produced

Since the cosmic rays themselves don’t point back to their sources, we look instead for neutrinos, a type of subatomic particle that should be produced as a byproduct of cosmic ray acceleration, wherever it’s happening
Neutrinos are very strange – they’ve been called ghost particles
They very rarely interact with other matter, so to see them, you need a very large detector
Our telescope is called IceCube because we use a cubic kilometer – a billion tons – of the Antarctic ice cap to catch neutrinos
One of IceCube’s 91 strings of sensors, called DOMs (digital optical modules), is lowered into the ice
They’re vertically spaced about 55 feet (17 meters) apart and meant to catch the visual repercussions of a neutrino collision

Jim Haugen, IceCube/NSF , CC BY-NC Most neutrinos pass invisibly through IceCube, but by chance a few of them will smash into a proton or neutron in the ice, releasing a shower of high-energy electrons, photons and other particles the detectors can see

By measuring the number and direction of these visible particles, we can determine the direction the original neutrino came from, its energy and its type, also called its “ flavor .” One by one, we build up a picture of the sky as it shines in neutrinos, rather than starlight
Halzen proposed the idea of building a neutrino telescope in Antarctica in 1988
The South Pole may not sound like the obvious place to build such a telescope, but in fact it’s the easiest place to do it
The United States maintains a scientific facility there , home to several other experiments besides IceCube
Most importantly for us, the South Pole station sits on top of nearly 1.8 miles (3 kilometers) of the purest, clearest ice in the world – a perfect neutrino target just waiting to be used
Planes need skis to land and take off at the South Pole
Mark Krasberg, IceCube/NSF , CC BY-NC Good for science, tough for people But “easiest” is not the same as “easy” – the South Pole is a challenging place to work
Traveling to the pole from the U.S. usually takes a week or more
The last leg of the trip is on a special ski-equipped LC-130 cargo aircraft, operated by the Air National Guard, which lands on a runway made of compressed snow

These aircraft can only reach the pole for four months of the year: at midsummer – January in the Southern Hemisphere – the average temperature is a balmy minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 26 degrees Celsius), but by March, temperatures have fallen to minus 50 F (minus 45 C), too cold for LC-130s to operate
Two ‘winter-overs’ toast the return of the Sun
Martin Wolf, IceCube/NSF We pack our work into those summer months, then hand IceCube off to two hardy “winter-over” scientists
Our winter-overs are part of a team of 45 people who stay at the station for the rest of the year, cut off from the rest of the world for eight months except for internet and radio communications
In the summer, the station population expands to around 150 people
The South Pole is a high-altitude desert, so the air is thin and very, very dry

title: Flu season is near – here’s a guide to available vaccines
url:
<title>Flu season is near – here’s a guide to available vaccines</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764250/original/file-20261006-50-gzpora.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5255%2C3503&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Several flu vaccine options are available, including a new one that&#39;s mRNA-based, the first of its kind. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/walgreens-sign-advertising-free-flu-shots-is-seen-outside-a-news-photo/2290459839">NurPhoto/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The number of people sick with flu is starting to increase across the United States, with health authorities warning that in some <a href="https://www.cdph.ca.gov/Programs/CID/DCDC/Pages/RespiratoryVirusReport.aspx">western regions</a> of the country, the 2026-27 flu season may be off to an early start.</p>

<p>Health authorities often advise people to get their <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/65over.htm">flu vaccine by the end of October</a> – but as an <a href="https://ph.ucla.edu/about/faculty-staff-directory/annette-regan">epidemiologist focusing on vaccines and infectious diseases</a>, I see the uptick in activity as a sign that there’s no time like the present. </p>

<p>Several vaccine options are available, including the new <a href="https://www.vaccineadvisor.com/news/fda-approves-mflusiva-mrna-influenza-vaccine/">mRNA influenza vaccine</a>, approved by the Food and Drug Administration in <a href="https://www.fda.gov/media/194121/download">August 2026</a>. </p>

<h2>Seasonal patterns</h2>

<p>It’s too early to say for sure that this year’s flu season will be an early one across the entire U.S. or to predict if it will be particularly severe. </p>

<p>As of Sept. 26, the latest date for which data is available, seasonal influenza activity remains <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/usmap.html">low nationally</a>, and wastewater surveillance still shows <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/wastewater/respiratory-viruses/national.html">very low to low activity</a> in most states.</p>

<p>However, the number of patients with respiratory infections who were testing positive <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/fluview/surveillance/2026-week-38.html">began increasing near the end of September</a>, suggesting that influenza viruses are beginning to circulate more widely.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/U1a51_b5Ibk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Basic steps like washing your hands and wearing a mask when you’re sick can protect the people around you during flu season.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the U.S., influenza typically starts to circulate during the fall and often <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/about/season.html">peaks sometime between December and February</a>. Factors such as which flu viruses are spreading, how closely those viruses resemble the ones targeted by the vaccine, and how much immunity exists in the community can all influence the <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu-burden/php/surveillance/index.html">timing, severity and overall impact of a flu season</a>. </p>

<p>The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention classified the 2025-2026 flu season as <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/us/articles/2026-01-05/us-cdc-says-2025-26-flu-season-moderately-severe-as-cases-hit-11-million">moderately severe</a>, with over <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu-burden/php/php/data-vis/2025-2026.html">32 million cases</a>,  390,000 hospitalizations and up to 81,000 deaths. Flu cases increased in November and <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nrevss/php/dashboard/index.html">quickly peaked in December</a>.</p>

<p>Health authorities partly attributed the moderately severe season to <a href="https://www.usnews.com/news/us/articles/2026-01-05/us-cdc-says-2025-26-flu-season-moderately-severe-as-cases-hit-11-million">low flu vaccination rates and poor match to last season’s vaccine</a>. </p>

<h2>Available flu vaccines</h2>

<p>Vaccination provides the best protection against influenza. <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccine-types/index.html">Several safe and effective vaccines</a> are available this season. </p>

<p>The CDC has released <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/hcp/vax-summary/seasonal-influenza-vaccines.html">interim guidelines</a> for this year’s flu season, recommending flu vaccines for most adults and children age 6 months and older. The <a href="https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/35699/AAP-updates-flu-guidance-adds-detailed?autologincheck=redirected">American Academy of Pediatricians</a>, the <a href="https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/practice-advisory/articles/2025/08/influenza-in-pregnancy-prevention-and-treatment">American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists</a>, the <a href="https://www.aafp.org/media-center/press-releases/aafp-announces-fall-immunization-recommendations-to-protect-patients-and-communities">American Academy of Family Physicians</a> and the <a href="https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/Seasonal-RTI-Vaccinations-in-Immunocompromised-Patients/">Infectious Diseases Society of America</a> also recommend flu vaccines for children and adults this year. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.aarp.org/health/conditions-treatments/older-adults-high-dose-flu-shot/">Enhanced vaccines</a> –  including higher dose and <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccine-types/flublok-vaccine.html">lab-grown</a> vaccines as well as vaccines containing ingredients that help the body produce a stronger immune response – are available for adults age 65 years and up and are designed to provide stronger immune responses. All are administered as injections. </p>

<p>Additional options include <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccine-types/nasalspray.html">FluMist</a>, a nasal spray vaccine approved for people age 2 through 49 – which may be preferable to those who want to avoid a shot.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccine-types/cell-based.html">Flucelvax</a> is a flu vaccine made using mammalian cells rather than eggs that is approved for people 6 months and older. However, people with an egg allergy <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccines/egg-allergies.html">can receive any flu vaccine</a> – even ones produced in eggs.</p>

<p>One new option this year is <a href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2026/how-the-mrna-flu-vaccine-compares-to-traditional-shots">mFLUSIVA</a>, the first mRNA-based influenza vaccine, approved by the FDA for adults age 50 and older. Because mFLUSIVA is so new, many vaccination sites may not yet offer it. People interested in receiving this vaccine should check with their local pharmacy, healthcare provider or <a href="https://products.modernatx.com/finder">Moderna’s online vaccine locator</a> for availability.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.ama-assn.org/public-health/prevention-wellness/doctors-united-respiratory-virus-vaccine-recommendations">Talk with your doctor</a> or healthcare provider if you have any questions about what vaccines are best for you and your family. </p>

<h2>Special protection</h2>

<p>Vaccination is especially important for those 65 years and older, young children, pregnant people, people with chronic medical conditions and those with weakened immune systems. These groups are at <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/flu/vaccines/vaccinations.html">greater risk of serious complications</a> from influenza. </p>

<p>Many people who are at higher risk of severe flu are also at higher risk of severe COVID-19, and the virus causing COVID-19 continues to <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/nrevss/php/dashboard/index.html">circulate</a>. Updated COVID-19 vaccines became available in September and can be given at the <a href="https://www.aarp.org/health/drugs-supplements/when-to-get-vaccines/">same clinic visit</a> with the flu vaccine. </p>

<p>Because it takes about two weeks for protection to develop after vaccination, getting vaccinated before flu activity becomes widespread provides the best chance of being protected when exposure risk increases.</p>

<p>This year, all three components of the influenza vaccines were <a href="https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/recommended-composition-of-influenza-virus-vaccines-for-use-in-the-2026-2027-northern-hemisphere-influenza-season">updated to better match </a> the viruses expected to circulate during the 2026-27 flu season. </p>

<p>While influenza vaccine effectiveness <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2026.18126">varies from year to year</a>, vaccination consistently <a href="https://vaxintegrity.cidrap.umn.edu/2026-27-respiratory-season">reduces the risk and severity</a> of influenza illness. If the flu viruses don’t change much over the course of the season, this year’s vaccines should provide protection that is similar to or better than what we’ve seen in recent years.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293480/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

She consults for the Pan American Health Organization and is affiliated with Kaiser Permanente Southern California.</span></em></p></content>

<title>Columbus’ own writings reveal how tightly religion and conquest were intertwined from the start</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763681/original/file-20261002-60-e8zphx.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C80%2C2304%2C1536&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A manuscript with the text of the letter Cristopher Columbus wrote in February 1493, giving his account of the first voyage to the Americas.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carta_Colon_1493_manuscrito_Simancas.JPG">Archivo General de Simancas/Spanish Ministry of Culture via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Few historic figures are as divisive as Christopher Columbus. For some, <a href="https://patrimonioypaisaje.madrid.es/portales/monumenta/es/Monumentos-y-Edificios-Singulares/Monumentos/Cristobal-Colon/?vgnextfmt=default&amp;vgnextoid=4c08091d1b9c4510091d1b9c45102e085a0aRCRD&amp;vgnextchannel=8fac3cb702aa4510VgnVCM1000008a4a900aRCRD">in both Spain</a> and <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/03/23/nx-s1-5757281/christopher-columbus-trump-white-house">the United States</a>, he remains <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/02/us/politics/trump-garden-of-heroes-national-statues-list.html">a great hero</a>, an explorer who found a “new world.” He is reviled by others who see him as an arrogant conqueror: <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/history-resources/essays/indian-slavery-americas">the first European to enslave Indigenous Americans</a>, and the man who launched <a href="https://archive.org/details/conquestofpa00sale/page/n3/mode/2up">ecological destruction in the Western Hemisphere</a>. </p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.petercmancall.com/">a historian</a> who writes about early encounters between Europeans, Indigenous Americans and Africans in North America, I believe it is important to recapture this period as much as we can from existing documents – including Columbus’ own writings. Those texts reveal the enormous importance the push to spread Christianity played in Europeans’ colonial plans from the start.</p>

<p>In <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/contested-continent-9780195372786">my 2026 book</a>, “Contested Continent: The Struggle for North America, c. 1000-1680,” I describe how Europeans’ religious desires shaped the creation  of American colonies that benefited conquerors, at a high cost to those they displaced or enslaved. In the Americas, the linkage of religious purpose and the eager pursuit of glory and wealth began in 1492. </p>

<h2>Before Columbus</h2>

<p>Long before Columbus set sail, Europeans were already eager to expand their faith – and territory. Centuries earlier, <a href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/jay-rubenstein/armies-of-heaven/9780465027484/?lens=basic-books">Crusaders had ridden into the Middle East</a> to reclaim what they saw as their holy land from Muslims.</p>

<p>That contest took place in Spain as well. Muslim armies had invaded from North Africa in the 700s, and Muslim rulers eventually governed much of the peninsula. Spanish and Portuguese leaders waged <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/Reconquista">the Reconquista</a>, a centuries-long war that concluded with the 1492 <a href="https://mjhnyc.org/blog/1492-letter-regarding-jewish-property-in-spain/">expulsion of Jews</a> and the defeat of the last Muslim stronghold in Granada.</p>

<p>By then, the Portuguese had laid claim to uninhabited mid-Atlantic islands, <a href="https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1758/the-portuguese-colonization-of-the-azores/">including the Azores</a> <a href="https://daily.jstor.org/madeira-the-island-that-helped-invent-capitalism/">and Madeira</a>. </p>

<p>They also colonized the Canary Islands and forced <a href="https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1002/ajpa.22879">local inhabitants</a> into slavery on their plantations. In 1479, Portugal ceded control of the <a href="https://dn760000.eu.archive.org/0/items/europeantreaties01daveuoft/europeantreaties01daveuoft.pdf">the Canary Islands</a> to Spain in a treaty to end a war between the two nations. Spaniards expanded <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/14788810.2017.1315514">the importation of enslaved Africans</a> to produce sugar. </p>

<h2>First voyage</h2>

<p>Columbus wanted to find the fastest way to get to the southwest Pacific <a href="https://www.bbc.com/future/bespoke/made-on-earth/the-flavours-that-shaped-the-world/">to bring home exotic spices</a>. He searched for sponsors to support his idea that Europeans could reach the the Spice Islands by sailing west across the Atlantic. Spain’s Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon provided funds to fit out three ships. </p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A black and white sketch shows men in armored hats standing on the shore as they talk with a group of unclothed men, while others raise a cross in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=629&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=629&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763684/original/file-20261002-50-vzf1fe.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=629&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>After his return, Columbus <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/sites/default/files/inline-pdfs/t-01427.pdf">wrote a letter to his patrons</a>, describing how, after 33 days at sea, <a href="https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/october-12/columbus-reaches-the-new-world">he landed in the Bahamas</a>. He labeled the people he met “Indios” because he thought he had reached Asia. The name stuck even though he was wrong about his point of arrival.</p>

<p>On his first voyage, Columbus claimed and renamed multiple islands, starting with San Salvador, or “Holy Savior.” “To the first of them I have given the name of our blessed Saviour, (with) whose aid I have reached this and all the rest,” <a href="https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/07fda820-0035-0130-671f-58d385a7bc34?canvasIndex=0">he wrote</a>. He named places after his patrons, too, along with other Christian names, such as Santa Maria de Concepion – Holy Mary of the Conception – and Navidad, Nativity.</p>

<p>He also laid claim to at least some Tainos. “I took by force some Indians from the first island,” <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/The-Columbus-papers-:-the-Barcelona-letter-of-1493-the-landfall-controversy-and-the-Indian-tribes-:-a-facsimile-edition-of-the-unique-copy-in-the-New-York-Public-Library/oclc/502565438">he wrote</a>, reporting that he wanted to teach them Spanish so they could “tell us what they knew” about environments new to him. </p>

<p>Soon after he returned to Spain, <a href="https://digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/07fda820-0035-0130-671f-58d385a7bc34?canvasIndex=0">Columbus had the text printed</a>. He wrote that “the whole of Christendom should rejoice” at discoveries he had made for his patrons “for all the glory they will receive when so many peoples turn to our Holy Faith.”</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A dark painting of a balding man wearing black clothes." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=717&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=717&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=717&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=901&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=901&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763687/original/file-20261002-50-az2zog.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=901&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Christopher_Colombus._Giovio_Musaeum.jpg">Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Within a few short years his words spread across Europe, translated from one language into another. Ferdinand and Isabella named him “<a href="https://www.loc.gov/exhibits/1492/columbus.html">Admiral of the Ocean Sea</a>.” </p>

<p>Columbus returned to the islands on three subsequent journeys. On the second, he dispatched <a href="https://www.dukeupress.edu/an-account-of-the-antiquities-of-the-indians">a friar named Ramón Pané</a> to live among the people of Hispaniola, record their beliefs and find strategies for converting them to Christianity.</p>

<h2>Conquest and Christianity</h2>

<p>Word soon spread that Columbus had allowed <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-other-slavery-andres-resendez?variant=67633849073698">forced labor</a> <a href="https://lareviewofbooks.org/article/a-plea-for-isabella/">of Indigenous peoples</a>. In 1500, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/summary/Christopher-Columbus-Timeline">he returned to Spain in chains</a> to face charges of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2006/aug/07/books.spain">incompetent administration of the colonies</a> and enslaving subjects of the realm.</p>

<p>Eager to get back into his patrons’ good graces – especially Isabella’s, <a href="https://press.vatican.va/content/salastampa/en/bollettino/pubblico/2024/09/19/240919h.html">since she was the most alarmed at his actions</a> – he became consumed by the history and theology of the church. He studied scripture as well as the writings of prominent theologians, including <a href="https://theconversation.com/st-augustine-was-no-stranger-to-culture-wars-and-has-something-to-say-about-todays-242372">St. Augustine</a> and the 15th-century French <a href="https://bridwell.omeka.net/exhibits/show/sciencereligion/pierredailly">cardinal and astrologer Pierre d'Ailly</a>. </p>

<p>Like a magpie on a spiritual quest, Columbus transcribed portions from the Bible and scholars into a kind of <a href="https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/collex/exhibits/book-use-book-theory-1500-1700/parts-and-wholes-matter-method/commonplace-thinking/">commonplace book</a> – a journal where he recorded parts of scripture and other writings, including his own notes. He intended the book for his queen and king, though it is likely they never saw it. </p>

<p>Nonetheless, their condemnation softened and they gave him permission to return to the Indies. He probably took the book along on his fourth journey of 1504. His son Ferdinand, who promoted his father’s legacy, called it <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Christopher-Columbus/Principal-evidence-of-travels#ref391415">the “Book of Prophecies</a>.”</p>

<figure class="align-left zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four figures in robes, including an infant, are positioned in front of an ornate building facade, while angels fly overhead." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=654&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=654&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=654&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=822&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=822&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763680/original/file-20261002-50-u2juy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=822&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Columbus told a powerful tale <a href="https://archive.org/details/bookofprophecies03colu/page/n7/mode/2up">in its pages</a>. He believed that God had endowed him with remarkable intelligence, despite enemies’ allegations that he was “an uneducated man, an uninformed sailor, an ordinary person.”</p>

<p>Columbus compared his struggles with those of biblical prophets, saying he was like Isaiah, who “was not just a prophet, but also an evangelist” who called “all people to our holy Catholic faith.” He wrote about the discovery of islands and converting “all peoples and nations.” He reported that the Roman historian Seneca had prophesied that “a large landmass” would appear during “the last years of the world,” adding that a “new sailor” would “discover a new world.”</p>

<p>In this book, which was not published in his lifetime, Columbus recast the renaming and charting of Caribbean islands <a href="https://archive.org/details/bookofprophecies03colu/page/4/mode/2up">as a religious pursuit</a>. He used Scripture to try to understand its geography, specifically seeking the Mount Zion mentioned in the Bible. He believed he had uncovered the Caribbean’s secrets because he had divine support for his task. The explorer wanted his royal patrons to see his role in history as something foretold by the ancients.</p>

<h2>A complicated legacy</h2>

<p>Columbus’ reputation has suffered over the years, with greater focus on what followed his voyages, including the spread of enslavement and environmental destruction. As one scholar put it in 1992, amid commemorations of the 500th anniversary of his first journey, the explorer was “<a href="https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1993/01/28/adios-columbus/">mugged on the way to his own party</a>.”</p>

Smith, File</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In recent years, protesters have <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/11/arts/design/christopher-columbus-statues.html">torn down his statues</a> and splattered others with red paint. His defenders have dredged statues out of rivers and remounted them. Each side has focused on his actions and their impact rather than his writings.</p>

<p>In those texts, the conquest and colonization of the Western Hemisphere were inseparable from religious conversion. His actions echoed in subsequent generations, evident in other Europeans’ efforts to <a href="https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/matthew-avery-sutton/chosen-land/9781541646339/?lens=basic-books">spread Christianity in the Americas</a>. Catholic Iberians, English Anglicans and  Puritans, and French Huguenots all latched onto that same idea: the hemisphere should become integrated into Christendom.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291332/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>What is a professional patient advocate, and why might you need one?</title>
    <content type="html"><p>Imagine your mom has just been discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation center after hip replacement surgery. She has the paperwork, the facility’s address – and a long list of questions. Will her insurance cover her entire rehab stay? Does she have enough pain medication until she gets settled? Will the hospital transfer her prescriptions? Are they accurate?</p>

<p>Scenarios like this are exactly what patient advocates are trained to help with. They understand patients’ and families’ concerns, ensure their voices are heard by medical staff and interface with care teams, insurance companies and facility administrators. They also coordinate care, set up follow-up appointments and address potential gaps or blind spots in care.  </p>

<p>I <a href="https://campus.und.edu/directory/jennifer.schlinger">train social workers</a> – who often serve as patient advocates – to help people in a variety of settings, including hospitals and nursing homes. Earlier in my career, I served as a professional patient advocate supporting people in hospitals, home health and hospice.</p>

<p>A trained patient advocate can provide much-needed support for people on their healthcare journey. Here’s what you need to know to work with one most effectively.</p>

<h2>The evolving field of patient advocacy</h2>

<p>Patient advocacy emerged out of the Civil Rights Movement’s focus on individual protections and rights. In 1966, healthcare advocacy pioneer Ruth Ravich <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/amj.2025.7">founded the Department of Patient Representation</a> at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York – widely considered the beginning of the patient advocate role.</p>

<p>Historically, doctors made decisions for patients <a href="https://doi.org/10.1378/chest.11-0516">without fully involving them in their own care</a>. But during the 1960s and in subsequent decades, a growing patient rights movement embraced the importance of informed consent for honoring patients’ autonomy. Patient advocates arose as an <a href="https://scholarship.law.vanderbilt.edu/vlr/vol27/iss2/2/">important voice in this movement</a> by educating patients about their rights and helping them participate more fully in decisions about their healthcare. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman sits across the table from a man who is showing her something on a clipboard." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=316&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761030/original/file-20260921-50-1xa2iy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">Patient advocacy emerged from a growing focus on individual rights and protections.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For decades, “patient advocate” was a self-described title, not a standardized role. As the healthcare system became increasingly complicated, the need emerged for national standards on skills, ethics and best practices. In 2018, the <a href="https://www.pacboard.org/">Patient Advocate Certification Board</a> established basic requirements for patient advocates and created a professional certification, which is the only one available for this role in the U.S. </p>

<p>Certification is not required to be a patient advocate, but it indicates that a person has received specific training for the role. To become certified, patient advocates must <a href="https://www.pacboard.org/competencies/">pass an exam demonstrating</a> a knowledge of health and medical concepts, issues relating to paying for care, an understanding of the healthcare system, how to work collaboratively with patients and other areas of competency. They must complete continuing education to maintain certification.</p>

<p>Some healthcare professionals who serve as patient advocates are not certified and instead have learned relevant skills through their education or professional experiences. They may work in rural healthcare facilities, for instance, where they wear multiple hats as nurses or social workers who are also advocates. </p>

<h2>What does a professional patient advocate do?</h2>

<p>Patient advocates are trained to support, inform and guide patients through the healthcare system. They help explain medical information, such as a medication’s side effects or treatment options. They also make sure patients’ questions are answered and their concerns are addressed. </p>

<p>When a patient receives a referral to a specialist, a patient advocate can connect care across various healthcare providers, making sure details about the patient’s condition or care priorities don’t fall through the cracks and helping to arrange transportation to appointments. </p>

<p>Early in my career, for instance, I worked at a hospital with patients who were being discharged to their home or to a long-term care facility. I started by understanding each patient’s goals, assessing their living arrangements and the type of care they needed and identifying any concerns they had about their discharge plan. Before they left the hospital, I coordinated community supports or additional care they might need, such as home-delivered meals, home healthcare, and physical, occupational or speech therapy. </p>

<p>Patients often have family members who are advocating on their behalf – and <a href="https://theconversation.com/family-caregivers-can-help-shape-the-outcomes-for-their-loved-ones-an-icu-nurse-explains-their-vital-role-222396">family support is invaluable</a>. Working with a patient advocate can provide something different: a grounded, objective perspective, expert knowledge of the healthcare system and knowledge of resources that patients and family members may not be aware of. </p>

<p>Indeed, patient advocates interact closely with family members and friends who are involved in the patient’s care. As liaisons between the patient, family and healthcare providers, their job is to keep the patient’s needs, preferences, goals and values at the center of their care.</p>

<p>Working with a patient advocate can help patients feel more confident in making informed decisions. According to a 2023 survey by a nonprofit alliance called <a href="https://chcao.org/">the Coalition of Healthcare Advocacy</a>, 92% of patients and healthcare providers reported that working with a patient advocate <a href="https://chcao.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/White-Paperv4.pdf">positively affected patients’ care</a>.</p>

<h2>Understanding bills and insurance coverage</h2>

<p>Managing financial aspects of healthcare can be overwhelming for patients and family members, particularly in the midst of a health crisis. Medical bills are often impenetrable documents littered with complex codes and terminology, and sorting through charges and details about insurance coverage can feel intimidating, if not downright paralyzing. </p>

<p>A patient advocate can provide a knowledgeable outside perspective on these issues that’s not clouded by the urgency and emotional weight of illness. </p>

<p>Some patient advocates have specialized knowledge in medical billing, coding, insurance and other financial matters. They can answer questions about medical terms or clarify charges on a patient’s bill, review the bill for errors such as incorrect or duplicate charges and assist with figuring out insurance coverage and reimbursement. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/2Rkzqosn2RQ?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A healthcare advocate can help make sure that patient’s needs, preferences, goals and values remain at the center of their care.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>If necessary, they can also appeal claims by acting as a liaison between the patient, the healthcare facility and the insurance company. Patient advocates can also help patients work with a hospital to set up a payment plan, explore additional financial support or coordinate access to community resources. </p>

<p>If a finance-related question falls outside an advocate’s knowledge or expertise, they can help the patient identify the right people to talk to. </p>

<h2>Finding and working with a patient advocate</h2>

<p>Finding a patient advocate is not always as straightforward as it should be. </p>

<p>If you are unsure where to start, ask to speak with a hospital social worker or case manager. In some cases, an advocate’s services are provided by the healthcare organization or are covered by insurance, but in others, the patient or family must pay for them out-of-pocket.  </p>

<p>Many healthcare facilities, including Veterans Affairs, have patient advocates on staff. You can contact your local hospital or clinic and ask to be connected to their patient advocate. Alternatively, you can search for a patient advocate in your area through the <a href="https://www.cms.gov/medical-bill-rights/help/guides/patient-advocate">Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services website</a> or the <a href="https://nahac.com/directory-of-advocates">National Association of Healthcare Advocacy</a>. </p>

<p>If a certified patient advocate is not available within your healthcare facility, request to speak with a social worker. Social workers have the education and expertise to support patients and families, to connect them with resources and to advocate for patients’ needs.</p>

<p>Before meeting with a patient advocate, identify your main objectives – for example, preparing for a transition home, clarifying a treatment plan or understanding medication changes. Then, write down your main concerns and questions. The <a href="https://thecarepartnerproject.org/">Care Partner Project</a> offers checklists for questions to ask healthcare providers, prepare for doctor visits, evaluate senior living communities and more. Gather any relevant information, such as medication lists, medical records, insurance documents and medical bills. </p>

<p>When you meet a patient advocate you’re considering working with, you can feel out whether they are a good fit by asking about their professional background, areas of expertise, experience and credentials. Some questions you might start with include: </p>

<ul>
<li><p>What is your experience with cases like mine? (For example, patients being transferred to a rehabilitation center, if that is your situation.)</p></li>
<li><p>Can you provide an example of how you helped a patient or family work though a difficult healthcare situation?</p></li>
<li><p>How do you typically communicate with patients and families, and how often can I expect to hear from you? </p></li>
<li><p>How do you help patients speak up about their concerns and preferences to their healthcare providers?</p></li>
</ul>

<p>Finding a healthcare advocate you trust can make navigating a complex health situation much less overwhelming.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/281971/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why people keep looking for Noah’s Ark in a natural rock formation in Turkey: A scholar of early Christianity explains</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763716/original/file-20261002-50-pw9hcg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=138%2C0%2C684%2C456&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Some people believe the Durupınar formation is the fossilized remains of Noah&#39;s Ark.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Structure_Claimed_to_be_the_Noah%27s_Ark_near_the_Mount_Ararat_in_Turkey.jpg">Mfikretyilmaz via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A <a href="https://haberler.cumhuriyet.edu.tr/haber/18597-universitemiz-onculugunde-yurutulen-nuhun-gemisi-arastirmalarinda-heyecan-verici-ilk-sonuclar">team of researchers from Sivas Cumhuriyet University</a> in Turkey is investigating a long-standing claim: that a boat-shaped geological formation in the country’s east contains the remains of Noah’s Ark. </p>

<p>In <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%206-9&amp;version=NRSVUE">the biblical Book of Genesis</a>, God decides to destroy the world with a flood. Following God’s instructions, Noah builds an ark – a large wooden vessel – to save himself, his family and animals of every kind.</p>

<p>The formation in question, known as Durupınar, has been associated with Noah’s Ark for nearly 70 years. This new research team has attracted social media attention through a partnership with a separate U.S.-based Christian organization called <a href="https://www.noahsarkscans.com">Noah’s Ark Scans</a>. This group has promoted the Durupınar site as the resting place of Noah’s Ark since at least 2021.</p>

<p>Durupınar is a natural geological formation composed of sedimentary material rich in iron oxides. It is located near the town of <a href="https://www.britannica.com/place/Dogubayazit">Doğubayazıt</a>, just a few miles from the Iranian border.</p>

<p><a href="https://haberler.cumhuriyet.edu.tr/haber/18597-universitemiz-onculugunde-yurutulen-nuhun-gemisi-arastirmalarinda-heyecan-verici-ilk-sonuclar">Official statements from researchers involved in this project</a> say that laboratory analysis is still underway. Researchers have nevertheless described some preliminary findings as potentially consistent with a shiplike structure, while <a href="https://x.com/noahsarkscans/status/2097361261944008910">claims circulating on social media</a> have been more definitive, saying that scans have confirmed the formation is man-made and “100% not geological.”</p>

<p>Claims that the formation is man-made have also appeared in <a href="https://www.joe.co.uk/news/first-look-inside-real-site-of-noahs-ark-as-activists-warn-darwinism-will-be-dismantled-549264">British</a> and <a href="https://www.dailywire.com/news/researchers-make-astonishing-discovery-in-hunt-for-noahs-ark">American</a> <a href="https://www.dailymail.com/sciencetech/article-16173705/noahs-ark-durupinar-turkey-man-made.html">media coverage</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://vandeneykel.substack.com">As a scholar of early Christianity</a>, I study biblical texts and their interpretation. Certain claims about the Durupınar formation have been circulating for decades, and they offer an opportunity to examine how people read and interpret the biblical flood story.</p>

<p>To understand the current claims, it helps to ask how this formation came to be associated with Noah’s Ark in the first place.</p>

<h2>A boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey</h2>

<p>The Durupınar formation takes its name from the Turkish Army captain İlhan Durupınar, who noticed the formation’s boatlike shape while examining aerial photographs of the region in 1959. Because of its close proximity to a peak known since the Middle Ages as Mount Ararat, <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%208%3A4&amp;version=NRSVUE">which the Genesis flood account claims is the place that Noah’s Ark came to rest</a>, Durupınar wondered whether this formation might be the petrified remains of the ark, preserved in the landscape over time.</p>

<p>The following year, Durupınar joined a team sponsored by the Archaeological Research Foundation in the United States on an expedition to the site. Led by George Vandeman, a television evangelist, and Arthur Brandenberger, <a href="https://www.britannica.com/science/photogrammetry">a specialist who used aerial photographs to measure and map the landscape</a>, the team traveled to the site with the explicit goal of confirming whether it was, in fact, the petrified remains of the fabled Ark of Noah.</p>

<p>The expedition was the subject of a short article in the <a href="https://books.google.com/books?id=GE8EAAAAMBAJ&amp;pg=PA112&amp;source=gbs_toc_r&amp;cad=2#v=onepage&amp;q&amp;f=false">Sept. 5, 1960, issue of LIFE magazine</a>. The article noted that while one member of the expedition remained skeptical on whether nature alone could be responsible for a shape like this, the surveys conducted ultimately “revealed no sign that the object was man made.” The expedition therefore concluded that it was a natural geological formation. In other words, it wasn’t the petrified remains of the biblical Noah’s Ark.</p>

<h2>How Durupınar became Noah’s Ark</h2>

<p>In the wake of the 1960 expedition, interest in Durupınar waned, and the case was closed for a time. The site returned to public attention in the late 1970s, when <a href="https://ronwyatt.com">Ron Wyatt</a>, a nurse anesthetist and amateur archaeologist inspired by the LIFE article, traveled to Durupınar to investigate for himself.</p>

<p>While at the site, Wyatt conducted <a href="https://ronwyatt.com/discovery/noahs-ark">a series of tests</a> and eventually claimed that the formation was actually the remains of Noah’s Ark. He argued that radar and other scans showed evidence of walls, decks, petrified wood, metal fittings and other materials that one might expect to find in the ruins of a wooden ship. Wyatt was also intrigued by large stones near the site that he claimed would have hung from the boat and steadied it while it was afloat.</p>

<p>Wyatt was initially able to convince another amateur archaeologist from the U.S., David Fasold, that his claims were true. In fact, in 1988 Fasold <a href="https://archive.org/details/arkofnoah00faso">published a book</a> in which he argued that the Durupınar formation was Noah’s Ark.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large wooden ship surrounded by animals and people, mostly in pairs." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=471&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=592&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=592&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763493/original/file-20261001-50-ytwo4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=592&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Flemish painter Simon de Myle’s illustration of Noah’s Ark on Mount Ararat.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Noah%27s_Ark_on_Mount_Ararat_by_Simon_de_Myle.jpg">Sotheby's Paris, June, 23 2011 via Wikimedia Commons</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Fasold’s enthusiasm for the site was relatively short-lived, however, and not even 10 years after publishing his book on the topic he co-authored <a href="https://doi.org/10.5408/1089-9995-44.4.439">a journal article</a> with geologist Lorence Collins that overturned his earlier conclusions. After a full assessment of the available evidence, Fasold concluded that “the supposed Ark near [Doğubayazıt] is a completely natural rock formation. It cannot have been Noah’s Ark nor even a man-made model.”</p>

<p>Trained geologists have tended to agree with the assessment of Fasold and Collins: Durupınar is a natural geological formation rather than the remains of a wooden ship. Geologist Murat Avcı, for example, identifies the boat-shaped feature as a large block of limestone that moved downslope in a landslide and was subsequently <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10064-007-0084-3">shaped by an earthflow and other geological processes</a>.</p>

<p>Geological analyses identified the material that Wyatt described as petrified wood as <a href="https://doi.org/10.5408/1089-9995-44.4.439">ordinary rock</a>, and the objects described as iron brackets as weathered volcanic material. The patterns that were interpreted as compartments of the ark are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10064-007-0084-3">consistent with the formation’s natural structure and fracturing</a>, while the proposed “anchor stones” are actually made of local volcanic rock.</p>

<h2>New research, ancient myth</h2>

<p>All of the results from the most recent research project are, <a href="https://www.cumhuriyet.edu.tr/haber/18523-akademisyenimiz-prof-dr-cenker-atila-onculugunde-dev-proje-nuhun-gemisi-arastiriliyor">at the moment, still preliminary and inconclusive</a>. Samples are waiting to be analyzed in labs, and official communications from the university say that evaluation of the evidence will continue into 2027.</p>

<p>As a biblical scholar, though, I am more interested in our ongoing fascination with flood stories.</p>

<p>Most biblical scholars read <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%206-9&amp;version=NRSVUE">the story of the flood in Genesis</a> as part of a much older tradition of flood mythology from the ancient Near East. Writers in ancient Mesopotamia told several versions of a story in which the gods send a catastrophic flood but warn one man, who then builds a large boat to save his family and animals.</p>

<p>In the <a href="https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_1889-0426-236">Atrahasis Epic</a>, for example, known from manuscripts dating back to the second millennium B.C.E., that survivor is Atrahasis. Another version of the same story also appears in the <a href="https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/W_K-3375">Epic of Gilgamesh</a>, where the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/Utnapishtim">flood survivor Utnapishtim</a> builds a large boat to weather the storm.</p>

<p>Genesis does not simply copy these older stories; it reshapes them. In Atrahasis, noisy humans become annoying to the gods, so the gods drown them. <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%206%3A11-13&amp;version=NRSVUE">Genesis, on the other hand, presents violence and corruption as the chief problem</a>. The ending of Genesis also moves in a different direction. Rather than imposing new limits on human reproduction, as the Atrahasis epic does, God in Genesis blesses Noah’s family, tells them to “be fruitful and multiply,” and <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%209%3A1-17&amp;version=NRSVUE">establishes a covenant with all of humankind and every living creature</a>.</p>

<p>One of the more interesting things about the flood story in Genesis is that the flood actually fails to solve the problem that caused it in the first place. Before the flood, humankind is inclined toward evil. After the flood, <a href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Genesis%208%3A21&amp;version=NRSVUE">the problem is still there</a>. But the story isn’t ultimately about eliminating human wickedness; it is about how life goes on despite humankind’s enduring flaws.</p>

<p>The current search at Durupınar, like those that came before it, assumes that behind the biblical story there is tangible evidence just waiting to be found. For nearly 70 years this boat-shaped formation has kept that possibility alive.</p>

<p>Ancient flood stories and how they changed across cultures can reveal how people made sense of catastrophe, human violence and the possibility of starting over. A boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey probably cannot.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293310/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Some people believe the Durupınar formation is the fossilized remains of Noah's Ark

Mfikretyilmaz via Wikimedia Commons , CC BY A team of researchers from Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey is investigating a long-standing claim: that a boat-shaped geological formation in the country’s east contains the remains of Noah’s Ark
In the biblical Book of Genesis , God decides to destroy the world with a flood
Following God’s instructions, Noah builds an ark – a large wooden vessel – to save himself, his family and animals of every kind
The formation in question, known as Durupınar, has been associated with Noah’s Ark for nearly 70 years
This new research team has attracted social media attention through a partnership with a separate U.S.-based Christian organization called Noah’s Ark Scans
This group has promoted the Durupınar site as the resting place of Noah’s Ark since at least 2021
Durupınar is a natural geological formation composed of sedimentary material rich in iron oxides
It is located near the town of Doğubayazıt , just a few miles from the Iranian border
Official statements from researchers involved in this project say that laboratory analysis is still underway

Researchers have nevertheless described some preliminary findings as potentially consistent with a shiplike structure, while claims circulating on social media have been more definitive, saying that scans have confirmed the formation is man-made and “100% not geological.” Claims that the formation is man-made have also appeared in British and American media coverage
As a scholar of early Christianity , I study biblical texts and their interpretation
Certain claims about the Durupınar formation have been circulating for decades, and they offer an opportunity to examine how people read and interpret the biblical flood story
To understand the current claims, it helps to ask how this formation came to be associated with Noah’s Ark in the first place

A boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey The Durupınar formation takes its name from the Turkish Army captain İlhan Durupınar, who noticed the formation’s boatlike shape while examining aerial photographs of the region in 1959

Because of its close proximity to a peak known since the Middle Ages as Mount Ararat, which the Genesis flood account claims is the place that Noah’s Ark came to rest , Durupınar wondered whether this formation might be the petrified remains of the ark, preserved in the landscape over time
The following year, Durupınar joined a team sponsored by the Archaeological Research Foundation in the United States on an expedition to the site

Led by George Vandeman, a television evangelist, and Arthur Brandenberger, a specialist who used aerial photographs to measure and map the landscape , the team traveled to the site with the explicit goal of confirming whether it was, in fact, the petrified remains of the fabled Ark of Noah
The expedition was the subject of a short article in the Sept. 5, 1960, issue of LIFE magazine

The article noted that while one member of the expedition remained skeptical on whether nature alone could be responsible for a shape like this, the surveys conducted ultimately “revealed no sign that the object was man made.” The expedition therefore concluded that it was a natural geological formation
In other words, it wasn’t the petrified remains of the biblical Noah’s Ark
How Durupınar became Noah’s Ark In the wake of the 1960 expedition, interest in Durupınar waned, and the case was closed for a time
The site returned to public attention in the late 1970s, when Ron Wyatt , a nurse anesthetist and amateur archaeologist inspired by the LIFE article, traveled to Durupınar to investigate for himself
While at the site, Wyatt conducted a series of tests and eventually claimed that the formation was actually the remains of Noah’s Ark
He argued that radar and other scans showed evidence of walls, decks, petrified wood, metal fittings and other materials that one might expect to find in the ruins of a wooden ship
Wyatt was also intrigued by large stones near the site that he claimed would have hung from the boat and steadied it while it was afloat
Wyatt was initially able to convince another amateur archaeologist from the U.S., David Fasold, that his claims were true
In fact, in 1988 Fasold published a book in which he argued that the Durupınar formation was Noah’s Ark
Flemish painter Simon de Myle’s illustration of Noah’s Ark on Mount Ararat

Sotheby's Paris, June, 23 2011 via Wikimedia Commons Fasold’s enthusiasm for the site was relatively short-lived, however, and not even 10 years after publishing his book on the topic he co-authored a journal article with geologist Lorence Collins that overturned his earlier conclusions
After a full assessment of the available evidence, Fasold concluded that “the supposed Ark near [Doğubayazıt] is a completely natural rock formation

It cannot have been Noah’s Ark nor even a man-made model.” Trained geologists have tended to agree with the assessment of Fasold and Collins: Durupınar is a natural geological formation rather than the remains of a wooden ship

Geologist Murat Avcı, for example, identifies the boat-shaped feature as a large block of limestone that moved downslope in a landslide and was subsequently shaped by an earthflow and other geological processes
Geological analyses identified the material that Wyatt described as petrified wood as ordinary rock , and the objects described as iron brackets as weathered volcanic material

The patterns that were interpreted as compartments of the ark are consistent with the formation’s natural structure and fracturing , while the proposed “anchor stones” are actually made of local volcanic rock
New research, ancient myth All of the results from the most recent research project are, at the moment, still preliminary and inconclusive
Samples are waiting to be analyzed in labs, and official communications from the university say that evaluation of the evidence will continue into 2027
As a biblical scholar, though, I am more interested in our ongoing fascination with flood stories
Most biblical scholars read the story of the flood in Genesis as part of a much older tradition of flood mythology from the ancient Near East
Writers in ancient Mesopotamia told several versions of a story in which the gods send a catastrophic flood but warn one man, who then builds a large boat to save his family and animals
