<title>Does your sleep tracker get it right? A Pittsburgh neuroscientist weighs in</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761753/original/file-20260923-50-9c5xos.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2121%2C1414&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A growing share of people wear a tracking device to bed, hoping it can tell them something about how they slept.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-sleeping-peacefully-in-bed-using-a-smartwatch-royalty-free-image/2254395660?phrase=sleep%20tracker&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">andreswd/E+ Collection via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On a typical night, I go to bed wearing a tracking watch on one wrist and another type of tracker on the other wrist. Then I compare their sleep findings while I drink my morning coffee. </p>

<p>I direct the <a href="https://www.healthandhumanperformancelab.com/center">Center for Modern Digital Health</a> at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, where my team and I study how to use wearables to improve health and performance. My lab’s research has relied on consumer devices for years. I wear them for both science and pleasure, and I also wonder how much of what they tell me is true. </p>

<p>Apple’s <a href="https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2026/09/introducing-apple-watch-series-12-with-the-all-new-health-sensing-system/">newest watch</a>, announced Sept. 9, 2026, greets its wearers each morning with a single “readiness” number, built partly from how it thinks they slept. Apple says the redesigned sensors deliver the most accurate heart-rate tracking of any wearable, but independent labs have not yet confirmed that. </p>

<p>Given the growing popularity of sleep trackers, I think it’s worth asking whether a sensor on your wrist or finger can really tell you how your brain was sleeping last night.</p>

<p>Here’s what recent studies show when consumer wearables are tested against the gold standard, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-444-64032-1.00025-4">polysomnography</a>.</p>

<h2>Does it know when I was asleep?</h2>

<p>Polysomnography, which combines EEG, <a href="https://theconversation.com/a-century-after-the-eeg-was-discovered-it-remains-a-crucial-tool-for-understanding-the-brain-213843">or electroencephalogram</a>, with other sensors, records brain waves, eye movements and muscle tone while a person sleeps.</p>

<p>On the simplest question – asleep or awake – today’s devices come close. A 2025 meta-analysis of 24 studies and nearly 800 participants found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.11460">wearables typically overestimate total sleep time</a> by about 17 minutes compared with polysomnography. In an eight-hour night, that’s an error of under 4%, roughly two taps of the snooze button.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A wrist with a sleep tracking device showing a sleep score." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761757/original/file-20260923-50-upmy3a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Wearable devices can estimate total sleep time fairly accurately, but sleep-stage tracking is a tougher science.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sleep-tracking-functions-on-fitbit-sense-health-tracking-news-photo/1276632208?adppopup=true">Gado/Smith Collection via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>That gap comes from a blind spot every wearable shares: quiet wakefulness. When you lie awake motionless in the dark, your tracker often mistakes it for sleep. If you sleep well, that rarely matters, because you don’t spend much time lying awake. But if you have insomnia, those long, still stretches add up, and your wearable is probably overestimating how much sleep you’re getting.</p>

<h2>Does it know what my brain was doing?</h2>

<p>I will start with the obvious: That wearable on your arm or finger does not measure your brain. It measures your heart rate, the beat-to-beat variability of that heart rate, your movement and your skin temperature. The bet the wearable companies are making is that the different sleep stages we go through at night leave trace fingerprints on all of these – <a href="https://www.thensf.org/what-is-rem-sleep/">REM sleep</a>, for instance, has a distinctive cardiovascular profile – and the wearable’s algorithm reads those sleep fingerprints and makes an educated guess about which stage you are in.</p>



<p>How good is that guess? A 2025 study of six wrist devices worn by 62 adults <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleepadvances/zpaf021">found only modest agreement with polysomnography</a> on sleep stages, along with significant gaps on time awake after falling asleep and on sleep efficiency. The authors concluded the better-performing watches could track “prolonged and significant changes in sleep architecture.”</p>

<p>Translation: Your deep-sleep number is a noisy nightly estimate, best used to identify significant changes in your sleep over time.</p>

<h2>What trackers get right</h2>

<p>One of my lab’s findings comes from using these devices for what they’re good at. In a 2023 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, we used Fitbits to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2209123120">track the sleep of more than 600 first-year students</a> at three universities, including Carnegie Mellon University. We found that a student sleeping six or fewer hours a night early in the semester had a lower end of term grade-point average relative to their previous semester – an effect that held even after we accounted for academic load and daytime naps. </p>

<p>Nightly sleep duration is the number these devices track well, and it’s the one my students can actually do something about, mostly by getting to bed earlier.</p>

<p>In a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleep/zsad167">2023 randomized trial</a>, 113 adults with insomnia symptoms spent five weeks in one of two groups. One group got feedback on their sleep as measured by a wearable sensor, along with guidance on how to interpret it. The other got <a href="https://theconversation.com/we-paid-college-students-about-5-a-night-to-sleep-at-least-7-hours-and-their-grades-quickly-improved-289935">standard sleep-hygiene</a> education: general advice on habits such as keeping a regular bedtime, cutting back on caffeine and screens, and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet.</p>

<p>The feedback group ended up reporting milder insomnia symptoms than the sleep-hygiene group, but the measured amount of sleep they were getting was unchanged. They weren’t sleeping longer, falling asleep faster or waking less. The researchers expected the data to correct a common pattern in insomnia: People often report sleeping less than the sensors record. The feedback didn’t shrink that gap any more than the sleep-hygiene sessions did. What changed was how troubled people felt about their sleep: The feedback group ended up less troubled by it, even though the sleep itself stayed the same. </p>

<p>That distinction between measured sleep and felt sleep is one that sleep scientists here in Pittsburgh have shaped for decades. Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh developed the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/0165-1781(89)90047-4">Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index</a> in 1989, a questionnaire that asks people to rate how they slept rather than measuring it with wearables. It remains one of the most widely used sleep measures in the world.</p>

<p>The trial’s results suggest that for many people, a wearable’s biggest effect is on the score that the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index measures: subjective feelings of one’s sleep quality.</p>

<p>A 2026 trial of 229 older adults in Japan <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/ggi.70756">points the same way</a>. Everyone got regular reports from a sleep monitor placed under their bedding. Participants who got the reports alone saw no improvement in their insomnia scores, but those who also got monthly phone guidance on sleep habits and daytime activity did, at least over the first three months. As in the first study, what improved was how people rated their sleep.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Woman asleep with smartwatch on wrist." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761765/original/file-20260923-50-gxlhdo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In lab tests, sleep trackers diverged from clinical measurements by about 17 minutes per night.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-deeply-asleep-in-a-bright-room-with-a-health-royalty-free-image/2278885160">Alina Barilo/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>A wearable can tell you how much you slept; it can’t make you sleep more. That part is up to you, or to someone who helps you. </p>

<p>And for some people, the tracking itself becomes the problem. Sleep clinicians have a name for patients who lie awake worrying about their sleep score: <a href="https://doi.org/10.5664/jcsm.6472">orthosomnia</a>, a term coined in 2017 and <a href="https://doi.org/10.2147/NSS.S402694">still very much in use</a>. If checking your score reliably wrecks your morning, the device isn’t working for you.</p>

<h2>How I read my own numbers</h2>

<p>I read the sleep stages and readiness scores the way I read a weather forecast: a useful trend but a poor guide to any single night. And I keep in mind that by the time a study comes out, the device it tested <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sleepadvances/zpaf063">has often been replaced</a>. </p>

title: Will Trump’s diesel order do anything?
excerpt: Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order on diesel access at a rally in in Grand Island, Nebraska, on October 5, 2026. | Win McNamee/Getty Images This sto
body: Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order on diesel access at a rally in in Grand Island, Nebraska, on October 5, 2026. | Win McNamee/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to fix the diesel crisis he caused.  What’s happening? On Monday evening, Trump signed an executive order intended to lower diesel prices by temporarily expanding access to red-dye diesel.  What’s red-dye diesel? A kind of diesel usually reserved for farm and construction equipment and other off-road uses — and marked with a little bit of red dye to distinguish it from other diesel sold for use in on-road vehicles

Ordinarily, it’s tax-exempt and not available to on-road vehicles, but Trump is expanding access in a bid to bring down the overall cost of fuel ahead of the midterm elections.  Trump’s order defers payment on — but does not actually suspend — the federal tax on red-dye diesel for on-road vehicles through the end of the year, while also directing his Cabinet “to explore pathways to eliminate the obligation to pay the deferred taxes.”  What’s the context? Diesel prices are way, way up because of the Iran war

Currently, the national average price per gallon is $6.32, compared to $3.68/gallon one year ago.  Will this do anything to lower prices? Not very much, in all likelihood, for a whole slew of reasons ably explained here — including that the order can’t change the underlying reality of a global diesel shortage
Why does the price of diesel matter? Most people don’t use diesel to fill up their tank, but semitrucks shipping food and other goods around the country rely on it

That means that when diesel gets more expensive, nearly everything else does too , sooner or later.  Why does Trump care? This is best explained by the fact that Trump signed the executive order while on the campaign trail in Nebraska — ordinarily a comfortably Republican state that instead looks potentially in play for independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn.  High diesel prices have hit hard in Nebraska and other agriculture-heavy states like Iowa and Kansas, jeopardizing Republican Senate seats in all three

title: Democrats are poised to take the House. Then what?
excerpt: House Democrats rally on the steps of the US Capitol on November 12, 2025, in support of renewing Affordable Care Act tax credits. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call,
body: House Democrats rally on the steps of the US Capitol on November 12, 2025, in support of renewing Affordable Care Act tax credits. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images With 28 days until the midterms, polling suggests that Democrats have an excellent chance of taking back the House in November
Flipping the Senate , once considered a long shot, is starting to look realistic
Come November, the party may have majorities in both chambers that will give it far more leverage than in the first half of this Donald Trump presidency

If voters entrust them with power, though, how will Democrats use it? Their legislative options will be limited, with Trump still in the White House, but party leadership has gestured at a platform focusing on affordability, healthcare, and investigations into the Trump administration.  Still, many of the particulars are missing — which Puck News congressional correspondent Marianna Sotomayor says is by design

As Sotomayor explains, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the likely next speaker of the House, will want to present a unified front ahead of the election, which means no infighting over the messy details of policy
The real work can start after they take the House

To break it all down, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Sotomayor about how Democrats are feeling ahead of the midterms, the prospect of a Speaker Jeffries, and the Democratic to-do list
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
What are the vibes in the House around these midterms? The vibes, if you ask Democrats, are incredibly strong

If anything, it’s mostly Democrats trying to tell each other, “Don’t oversell how amazing of a night we’re going to have.” Genuinely, in the number of conversations that I’ve been having with strategists, lawmakers, those seeking office themselves, the question isn’t, “Will Democrats flip the House majority?” anymore
It’s “Democrats will flip the House majority
How big is that majority going to be?” They want to play in deep Trump districts, and they’ve been doing that in Trump +5, Trump +10 districts that he won in ’24

Now they’re like, “What about Trump +21 districts?” And some people are like, “Whoa, whoa, whoa, guys, let’s not get too overly excited” because everybody kind of has some PTSD from the ’22 midterms — that’s when Republicans ended up taking up the House. [In 2022], Republicans were in the same place around this time where they were like, “Oh my gosh, we’re going to flip 30-plus seats.” And then they only gained a five-seat majority
And we saw how difficult that [majority] was for Republicans, and frankly, it continues to be
You would think that the Democrats would be trying to sell themselves based on, “Here’s what we’re going to do if we flip the House and the Senate. ” But I don’t hear a ton of that
What are this party’s priorities if they take back the House? You’re totally spot-on
I’m sure Democrats would argue, no, we’re being really specific

And sure, we do know that if they take the majority, there’s three planks, and this is what Jeffries outlined even a year ago, and [Senate Minority Leader Chuck] Schumer, to some extent, has also adopted these planks
They want to tackle affordability, healthcare, and corruption
Affordability means a number of different things
And the way that Jeffries is looking at it is you have your first 100 hours, your 100 days, and then your first year

And we don’t really know what is going to come up in those 100 days and in the first year, but within those 100 hours, he’s starting to give us some hints.  There are some issues where they could easily, probably very quickly, pass
Those Medicaid tax credits that are going to expire just in the next couple of months because of the one Big Beautiful Bill, [for example]
You also have the corruption part of this where a number of committee Democrats have been taking notes

It’s like, oh, the Trump admin did that? Okay, going to write that down so I can remember to circle back when we have the majority.  I’ve been told to expect subpoenas to start being sent out to administration officials, to Cabinet officials, to potential corporations that have cozied up too close to the Trump administration, pretty much after the House majority is declared
Is it all but certain that Hakeem Jeffries will be Speaker if the Democrats win? From inside of the Capitol, all that I’ve heard is that he is going to be speaker

That being said, a number of progressives like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Delia Ramirez, a number of those members are already talking to a number of the progressives who are coming in, who are kind of being a little coy with whether they’re going to vote for Jeffries.  Their message has been, look, Democrats need to stay united
We have differences of opinions on a number of fronts, but we need to be united, we need to govern, and we can’t get to any of that until we elect a speaker
I remember Nancy Pelosi didn’t really want to spend the years of Trump’s first term investigating and impeaching, but the nature of Trump forced her to ultimately do that

Do you think Jeffries has learned anything from how his predecessor approached the president? To your question about impeachment, it is fascinating to see where House Democrats are right now versus where they were back then
I do not hear “let’s impeach Trump” that much from the 200 and something Democrats that are currently in office

And the reason why is because, one, there is the thinking that, okay, the Constitution says he can only be a two-term president, and probably the Supreme Court’s going to rule that he can’t run again [if he tries]

But because Democrats are already thinking, planning, strategizing all of their investigations, I think we should expect possible impeachments against Cabinet officials. [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth is a name I keep hearing a lot, because there’s a number of Republicans who are incredibly upset with him.  Democrats are thinking a little bit more strategically in terms of if we are going to impeach, or if we’re really going to try to subpoena or hold people in contempt of Congress, will we have Republicans backing us up in those certain cases?  These three planks — affordability, healthcare, and holding the crooks accountable — those could have been the planks in month one or month two of the second Trump term.  I wonder how much motivation there is in the caucus to take on some of the issues that have come up in the last year or so
ICE comes to mind, Iran, spending billions of dollars on vanity projects around DC, making billions of dollars off of his own name and brand while in office
How much are Democrats pushing for the issues that maybe have struck a chord more recently? Behind the scenes, actually, they’ve been pushing those things a lot
But my understanding is that Jeffries doesn’t necessarily want to broadcast anything that could show any divisions among Democrats right now

He really just wants to project that Democrats are united on these three issues.  Everybody else is like, okay, but there’s so many more things that we have to prove, and we should get done and we should show contrast with Republicans moving forward
And my understanding is his idea of it is we will get to those issues after the election
They’re not even worth debating pre-election because first we have to win

title: Movies may soon get more boring
excerpt: An activist protests the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros
body: An activist protests the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros

Discovery in Hollywood on September 22, 2026. | Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

The Trumpy tech billionaire Larry Ellison has wrapped his tentacles around the US branch of TikTok, an entire Hawaiian island — and now, officially, a very large share of the world’s news and entertainment production
On Tuesday, the media behemoth Paramount — which is headed by Ellison’s son — completed its $110 billion mega-merger with Warner Bros
Discovery, in a controversial and hard-fought deal backed by the elder Ellison
The merger combines a sprawling collection of brands, including HBO, CBS, and Paramount Pictures under one rebranded umbrella
It also concentrates much of the US film and television business in the hands of just five companies

Unions, theater owners, media watchdogs, and several state attorneys general were accordingly concerned: Combining two major competitors in any industry inherently concentrates power over what gets made, what consumers pay, and what workers earn
Critics of this deal argued that, in the media industry, the fallout could be particularly intense

In addition to layoffs , opponents warned the new company could produce fewer, more boring movies, raise subscription prices for its combined streaming services , and inject political bias into news programs on CBS and CNN. (We’ll review the evidence for some of these claims in a minute.)  The new company agreed to address some of these concerns in a September 21 settlement agreement with 12 state attorneys general, which let the merger proceed
A group of consumers also launched a last-minute bid to block the deal, but the Supreme Court declined their emergency request on Monday

Go a little deeper View Link One of the conditions of that September AG settlement was a minimum film guarantee: The merged company agreed to release at least 30 films a year for the first two years after the merger, then 32 films a year for three years after that
The requirement was designed to address one of the major fears around the deal: namely, that mergers can result in fewer films
Recent history, and the basic economics of acquisitions, help explain the concern
Debt-financed acquisitions, like this one, can leave companies under pressure to cut costs
There are a few ways to do that, such as producing fewer new films or cancelling unreleased films that they don’t want to promote
According to Cinema United, a theater industry group, Disney and 21st Century Fox put out about half as many theatrical releases after their 2019 merger as they did before it, excluding 2020 and 2021
But that doesn’t mean the new Paramount/Warner Brothers (formally rebranded Skydance) would do the same thing
Disney, for instance, makes a lot of its money from properties and products that  aren’t movies

When the European Commission took up the question of whether this new merger would reduce output earlier this year, it concluded that Paramount and Warner were comparatively more dependent on film revenue

In other words, cutting back the number of movies they make post-merger “would not make economic sense” the way it did for Disney after its acquisition.  Still, consolidation could certainly change  which movies get produced
Critics argue that fewer studios mean fewer opportunities for Hollywood creatives and less pressure on the remaining players to take creative risks

In  a report released over the summer , academics with the Media and Consolidation Research Organization at UC San Diego warned this particular deal would likely result in less diverse and more formulaic films
I, for one, won’t be holding my breath for a Larry Ellison biopic

But before you load up your cart, double-check that the sale is actually a good one…and that you truly want or need the item in question
The psychological rush of scoring a deal is so strong that it can lead you to buy things you never planned to purchase

title: America’s tallest, most spectacular trees are getting…heat stroke?
excerpt: A redwood tree grove at Roberts Regional Recreation area in Oakland, California. | Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images A grove of coast redwood trees is a fo
body: A redwood tree grove at Roberts Regional Recreation area in Oakland, California. | Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images A grove of coast redwood trees is a forest of forests
Individual trees can live for thousands of years, and as they grow, their canopies develop mats of soils and ferns, creating something like a second forest floor hundreds of feet above the ground

These elevated ecosystems are home to creatures like the wandering salamander , which can spend its entire life cycle on top of a single tree, and the marbled murrelet, a seabird whose nesting habits were a mystery until one day in 1974 , when a tree-trimmer stumbled upon a nest 150 feet above the ground

Sometimes a stray seed — a sitka spruce or oak or even another redwood — finds its way up a massive redwood and grows into another tree entirely, nestled among the branches of a giant.  For millennia, redwoods have been the anchors of this incredibly stable ecosystem; they can even survive wildfires that devastate other tree species
They’ve also been the source of plenty of human inspiration and drive millions of dollars to California’s tourist economy

But like other living things, they aren’t immune to warming temperatures, and it turns out these trees have a particular weak spot.  A new study from researchers at University of California Davis , using measurements taken twice a month for two years, found that coast redwood leaves essentially dial down their photosynthesis during periods of extreme heat
This means trees are slowing their “breathing” and “eating” because they can’t cool down fast enough when temperatures rise

It’s a problem that’s only going to get worse as climate change continues to drive global temperatures up, and it raises urgent questions about the future of these iconic trees and the layers of life that live on and around their shadow-dappled lengths.   How a redwood fasts To understand what’s happening to the redwoods — and what that may mean for the species that rely on them — first we need to take a quick foray into tree anatomy
Trees use the pores in their leaves, stomata, to do two things: take carbon dioxide in, and let water out
Open stomata mean the tree is “breathing” in carbon dioxide and photosynthesizing, but probably also letting water out

Closed stomata mean the tree is conserving water but also slowing down its photosynthesis, since it isn’t taking in any carbon dioxide.  “Because leaves are a physical, light-absorbing object, they heat up just like asphalt would in the sun,” said Lily Klinek , a PhD student at UC Davis who was the lead author on the study.  “They’re heating up faster than the air around them,” she said. “And one way that they can cope with this is by opening their stomata and allowing water to transpire out of the leaf, which is kind of like the way that humans sweat
When water evaporates off our skin, it cools us down, and it’s the same for leaves

But they can only really do that if they have enough water to lose.” Klinek and her colleagues studied coast redwoods in Mendocino County, near the southern part of their range, where the researchers used specialized instruments to measure whether or not individual leaves were photosynthesizing
During heat waves, they found, coast redwoods hit a point where they can’t cool down fast enough, and they just keep their stomata closed

While that saves water, it also means the tree isn’t taking in more carbon — which means it’s not “eating” or building up energy stores it can use to keep growing.  This may sound like a technicality of tree physiology

But it could have a big impact on these forests, creating a vicious cycle where trees don’t have enough carbon stored to replenish their leaves in the future, which means they won’t be able to photosynthesize as efficiently, which will starve them even further, repeating until trees eventually die

And while this sort of behavior has been observed in tropical trees, it’s the first time anyone has studied how coast redwoods respond to the same heat stress.  “The term people use is carbon starvation,” said Chris Still , a forest ecologist at Oregon State University who didn’t participate in the study. “Leaves can be expensive to build for a plant.”  Most of the redwoods in California and the Pacific Northwest nowadays are new-growth forests planted in the last couple of centuries

That means the trees are relatively hungry, like growing adolescents, compared to their old-growth cousins, so they need to suck in lots of carbon dioxide to grow taller.  Redwoods are also incredibly good at storing carbon

Thanks to their bulk and long lives, they store more carbon dioxide per acre than any other forest in the world. “Not only is it negative feedback on the climate system itself, with less carbon sequestration from these trees and forests, but the trees themselves are going to obviously not grow as big,” said Anthony Ambrose , a plant physiological ecologist and co-founder of the Ancient Forest Society

So even if the trees survive, they might not have as much space for fern and soil mats, which means less habitat for the creatures that live in them, and they may not grow as tall as they once used to, which could hurt them in another way.  The fog of old forests A central threat to these trees, Klinek explained, is that in addition to the heat stress, they may also lose a crucial source of hydration and protection: Coast redwoods have an intricate relationship with the fogs of their native Northern California and the Pacific Northwest
The trees are so tall that their canopies reach high into fog layers, where they can sip water directly from the sky
The fog also shades the trees from the sun and helps coast redwoods create their own microclimate, which is why these forests are noticeably cooler than the areas adjacent to them

But warmer oceans and drier air are making fog more sporadic, which means the trees are missing a crucial source of relief from heat that is only getting more intense.  “It’s kind of a double whammy,” said Todd Dawson , a plant ecophysiologist at the University of California Berkeley, who also didn’t participate in the study. “They’re running out of water and also getting this heat stress,” he said. “They’re used to living in a very narrow temperature range of 8 to 27 degrees Celsius (about 46 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit)

California, like everywhere, has been getting long periods of much warmer days than we’ve ever experienced, and now the fog, which is normally kind of like an air conditioner, has also declined between 30 and 40 percent.”  These temperature swings also impact the organisms living high up in the trees. “If they experience really excessive heat throughout the summer,” Ambrose said, “then the soil mats and ferns will probably dry out much faster
And then those salamanders and birds might not be able to live there

So we’ll see cascading effects through the whole ecosystem at that point.” Klinek said, the trees seem to be doing okay after the heat passes; while the leaves she and her team looked at over their two-year study didn’t acclimate to the heat, they also didn’t lose their capacity to photosynthesize after the heat passed

While that’s a bit of hopeful news, it doesn’t reduce the urgency of the need to better understand the impact of climate change on these trees, and to reduce the warming itself.  “Right now the temperatures are coming back to normal in the fall and winter and letting the trees recover,” Klinek said. “But in five or 10 years, if temperatures are even hotter and heat waves are even more frequent, we don’t really know if there would be a recovery.” For now, the salamanders and seabirds still have their homes high atop the coast redwoods
But we’re a part of the redwoods’ larger ecosystem too, even if we don’t live near them — they, like all trees, are key to keeping our planet hospitable
The trees Klinek studied have the potential to live for more than a thousand years

title: Trump’s plan to buy votes, briefly explained
excerpt: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images This
body: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is trying to bribe his way out of a midterm disaster.  What’s happening? Over the weekend, Trump announced a plan to send $90 payments to more than 20 million Americans 65 years and older, drawing from a pool of money called the Medicare Improvement Fund.  Trump, in a post, described the payments as part of a strategy to “substantially LOWER costs for our Seniors” — but the money, a single nonrecurring payment set to go out this month, was reportedly already earmarked for other programs before Trump decided to redirect it.  Why now? Trump, facing a potentially catastrophic midterms for his party, has been looking for any way to turn out (Republican) voters — up to and including offering them cash, either implicitly or explicitly, in return for their support.  In the implicit category: these $90 payments and a smaller number of $500 Affordable Care Act refunds (fewer than 1 million) that began going out last week.  Much more explicitly, however, he’s also promising Americans $5,000 if they reelect Republicans in the midterms

Trump has directly linked Medicare payments with the promised checks: “Because I delivered on this very important issue for the American People,” he wrote in a post, “they can also rest assured the highly popular $5,000 Trump Dividend will be distributed to every U.S

Citizen if, and when, the Republicans win the Midterm Elections!” Will it work? It’s hard to say for sure, but it feels unlikely: The Medicare payments are relatively small, while the ACA payments are going out to relatively few voters

Polling suggests that voters are not fans of the promised $5,000 checks, and even fewer believe that they’re going to happen (they’re almost certainly correct ).  What else should I know? Direct payments to Americans — real or promised — are not the only way Trump is trying to sway the midterms in his favor
He’s also continuing to spend taxpayer dollars on a propagandistic ad campaign , which he personally directed

title: What you should know about the Russian “plague lab”
excerpt: People stroll along the river in Irkutsk, Russia, where the recent death of a lab technician prompted quarantines. | Hao Jianwei/Xinhua via Getty Images This st
body: People stroll along the river in Irkutsk, Russia, where the recent death of a lab technician prompted quarantines. | Hao Jianwei/Xinhua via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

The death of a 28-year-old lab tech halfway around the world is not typically the sort of thing the White House monitors .  But when that tech dies of severe pneumonia…while working at a Siberian plague research lab…foreign governments (and pretty much everyone in my timeline) tend to pay more attention.   The World Health Organization says that there’s little cause for concern , to be clear
Testing has turned up no connection between the woman’s work and her cause of death.  And even if she did contract pneumonic plague, that’s hardly a doomsday scenario
The plague comes in three flavors — bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic — and they all crop up from time to time, particularly in places like Central Asia and Africa
If caught early, pneumonic plague is typically curable with common antibiotics

A man in Arizona caught the disease from his cat in 2025 , for instance, but didn’t spread it to anyone else.  Of course, the real fear (and the reason so many people are talking about this today, I suspect) is that Russia has, at various times in its history, worked to develop more deadly and contagious forms of plague for use as a biological weapon.  There’s no evidence linking that program to this lab or this death in Siberia
Still, the general threat of biological warfare is so ominous and urgent that now seems like a worthwhile time to understand it a bit better

Go a little deeper In her very recent and slightly spooky book, Biological War: A Scenario,  journalist Annie Jacobsen lays out how world governments and health authorities are poised to respond to the hypothetical leak of a weaponized pneumonic plague from a Russian lab
At the risk of being euphemistic here, let me say that she concludes things would not go well.  But wait! There’s even more doom and gloom where that thought experiment came from

AI chatbots have made it hypothetically possible for more-or-less ordinary people to grasp the research and techniques they’d need to hack together their own biological weapons.  Just last month, the AI giant Anthropic disclosed five cases where scientists had tried to use its software on research that could have been used in weapons development
And while the company apparently shut those attempts down, their mere existence is fairly frightening
Can anything be done about these risks, now that they’re here? My colleague Noel King asked Jacobsen that very question in early September
Jacobsen essentially said that the public needs to demand policies aimed at avoiding the “nightmare scenario,” whether that’s an inadvertent lab leak or terrorist attack
Such policies might include things like independent testing of AI models or stricter licensing requirements for high-risk labs.  But it’s unclear what authority could rein in bad state-level actors
And it’s hard to imagine a public upswell for such niche scientific regulations, particularly at a moment when we don’t lack for other doomsday threats
For now, I suppose, I’ll take (partial, provisional) solace in the fact that this Russian situation doesn’t look like one of them.  One link for later ➨ Curtail your catastrophizing

Catastrophizing is a common thought pattern where you assume the worst possible scenario. (For instance, perhaps you read about a quarantine in Russia and began to fear for the end of the world!) Catastrophic thinking can help prepare us for difficult or frightening situations, but it can also be a major source of stress

Try interrogating your doomsday thoughts and noting when the worst case doesn’t come to pass.  Before you go… Did you know… that, according to some physicists, glass defies categorization as a simple liquid, solid, or gas ? title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
excerpt: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has been charged with join
body: Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged, while whereabouts of other five remain unknown An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood
